events.text: Your house has kept one fire alive for nine generations. Every night it is banked in the old clay fire jar under a lid of ash, and every morning it is coaxed back up for the stove, and the grandmothers say the day it goes out the luck of the house goes with it. This winter the keeping is yours. On the coldest night of the year you wake with a start, and the kitchen is black, and the jar is cold to the touch. You dig in the grey ash with your fingers. Nothing. Then, right at the bottom, one red point. It is not an ember. It blinks.

choices.text: Blow on it, very gently, and feed it a pine needle

effects.log: You bend down and breathe on it, the softest breath of your life, and lay one dry pine needle across it. The needle curls and glows. The red point swells, and shakes itself, and something in the ash goes chirp, small and cross and perfectly clear. By dawn the stove is lit and the rice is on and nobody in the house knows anything happened. You know. You keep a little bundle of pine needles by the jar from that night on.

choices.text: Cup it in your bare hands and carry it to the stove

effects.log: You scoop it up, ash and all, in your cupped hands. It burns like a bee sting, then like a coal, and you do not let go. Six steps to the stove. You tip it onto the kindling and it catches at once, far too fast, and for one moment in the new flame you see a shape like a tiny bird, shaking out its feathers. Your palm blisters into a red mark the size of a coin. It never quite goes away. On cold days it is the only warm part of you. (-4 health)

choices.text: Run to the neighbours for fire

effects.log: You run barefoot over the frozen yard to the Pak house and beg a coal in a pot, which the old people say must never, ever be done. When you get back, the red point in the cold jar is still there, waiting. You tip the borrowed coal in beside it. The two fires sit side by side a moment, and then the little one hops, quite plainly hops, into the borrowed one, and the whole jar flares up red. Grandmother finds out by noon. She is furious, and then, looking at the fire, very quiet.

events.text: The first full moon, and every child in the village is out on the paddy dykes swinging fire cans: an old tin with holes punched in it, a few coals inside, on a long string, whirled round and round until it roars. It is to burn the rats out of the dykes, the grown-ups say, and the bugs, and the bad luck. Yours is the best can on the dyke. Then the string snaps. Your can goes sailing up over the dark, trailing sparks like a comet, and lands with a thump on the thatched roof of the widow Seo's house. The thatch starts to smoke.

choices.text: Climb up after it

effects.log: You go up the persimmon tree and onto the roof in your socks. The thatch is smoking in a ring round your can, and sitting IN the can, on the coals, as if it were a nest, is a small red bird no bigger than a sparrow, looking at you. It hops out. The smoke stops. Every spark goes out at once, as if called. The bird looks at you a moment longer, then flies off into the dark, and you have to be got down off the roof by the widow's son with a ladder.

choices.text: Shout for water and wake the village

effects.log: You shout until the whole village comes running with buckets. By the time the first bucket is up, there is no fire at all. The can is sitting on the ridge of the roof, cold, and on top of it a small red bird is sitting, preening, as if it had done nothing. It flies off over the heads of the whole village. Half of them saw it. The other half say you made the whole thing up. The boy from the next house says he is going to catch it.

choices.text: Stand still, and bow to whatever is on the roof

effects.log: You do not know why you do it. There is something red moving on the thatch, among the sparks, and you put your hands together and bow, the way you bow at New Year. When you look up, a small red bird is lifting your fire can off the roof by its broken string, in its beak, quite easily, and carrying it down to the frozen paddy, and setting it on the ice. Then it flies off. The widow Seo never knows how close it was.

events.text: You hold a beacon post on the southern coast this year: five stone chimneys in a row on a bare hill above the sea, a hut, a pile of pine and dried dung for each, and one rule. One fire each evening if all is well. Two, an enemy sighted. Three, near the shore. Four, landing. Five, battle. Tonight it is raining sideways off the sea and there are sails on the grey edge of the dusk, how many you cannot tell, and the beacon will not light. The wood is soaked. The next post is waiting for your smoke. Then a red bird drops out of the rain, straight down into the wet pile of the first chimney, and the pile catches with a sound like a breath. It looks at you, and waits.

choices.text: Light two: an enemy sighted, which is what you truly saw

effects.log: You carry fire from the first chimney to the second. Two fires. The red bird hops from one to the other, and both burn fierce in the rain. On the next hill, a long moment later, two answer. Then two on the hill after. In the morning the sails turn out to be a raiding fleet that saw the hills light up and thought better of it. The commander of the coast, reading the report, writes your name down for promotion and asks who lit the wet wood. You say you do not know.

choices.text: Light five: battle, so the capital will listen

effects.log: Five. You run from chimney to chimney with a burning brand, and the red bird runs beside you through the rain, and every pile it touches roars up. Five fires. On the next hill, five. And on the next, all the way up the coast and into the dark, five and five and five. By dawn the villages are empty, the soldiers are marching, and the sails are a fishing fleet from three counties sheltering from the storm. You are flogged. The red bird, you notice, sits on the hut roof and watches the whole flogging, without a sound.

choices.text: Light one: all is well, you are not sure, and false alarms are flogged

effects.log: One. All is well. The red bird looks at you, and then at the sails, and then at you again, and then it lifts out of the fire and flies off south into the rain, low over the sea, toward the sails. On the next hill, one fire answers: all is well. At midnight, far down the coast, a glow comes up red under the clouds where no beacon is. A village is burning. You see it from your hill all night. You will see it for the rest of your life.

events.text: Your sect elder has sent you to the medicine market in the southern port with a heavy purse and a strange order: "vermilion feather cinnabar," for writing talismans, from a particular old dealer in the last alley. Everyone in the sect knows it is a name for ordinary cinnabar, a dealer's boast. The old dealer looks at you a long time, goes to the back, and comes out with a lacquer box. Inside, on red silk, is one long tail feather, scarlet shading to gold at the tip, and it is warm. The silk under it is scorched. "Took me forty years to get it," the dealer says. "Write one charm with it and no ghost will come within a mile. Grind it, and you have ink for a thousand."

choices.text: Pay, and carry it home to the elder as ordered

effects.log: You pay ten taels and carry it home inside your jacket. It keeps you warm all the way through the hills, like a hand on your chest. Your elder opens the box, goes very still, and then begins to grind. The ink is a red so bright it hurts. The talismans written in it work: you see it with your own eyes, the night the hungry ghost at the north gate takes one look and goes. But somewhere south, you are fairly sure, something has noticed that a feather has gone into a mortar, and is asking where.

choices.text: Ask to hold it, and lay it in the dealer's brazier

effects.log: You ask to hold it. You walk to the dealer's charcoal brazier and lay the feather across the coals before anyone can stop you. The dealer screams. The feather does not burn. It brightens, and straightens, and lifts, and goes up out of the brazier in a little spiral of sparks, out through the smoke-hole in the roof and away south. The dealer sits down hard on the floor. You go home with an empty box and a full purse and a scolding, and the warm smell of it on your fingers for a month.

choices.text: Pay for it, and keep it yourself

effects.log: You pay ten taels of the sect's money and tell the elder the dealer had none. You keep the feather in your sleeve. It is warm on the coldest night. Water will not boil over when it is near. Once, in a bad inn, a dark thing came to the foot of your bed, and the feather in your sleeve glowed, and the thing went away. You feel, sometimes, that you are being looked for. Not angrily. As if by someone who would like their feather back, and will ask politely, once.

events.text: You have climbed alone to the highest peak of the southern mountains to sit out the hottest day of the year in meditation. At noon on the summer solstice the sky to the south goes red, and seven groups of stars you should not be able to see by day come down out of it together, and are one great bird of fire, and land. A table is set under its wings, long and low, with dishes from every southern province, and the smell of grilled fish and peaches. Guests sit along it, strangers in fine robes from very far away. One seat at the table is empty, the cushion scorched black. "Sit," says the bird, in a voice like a summer afternoon. "The south keeps a table for guests. That seat was set for one who burned." Everyone is looking at you.

choices.text: Before you sit, raise your cup to the empty seat

effects.log: You lift your cup to the scorched cushion, and bow to it, and set it down untouched, before you have sat down yourself. The table goes quiet. Then the great bird bows to you, its whole burning head down to the table, and the guests along the table, one by one, lift their own cups to the empty seat. It is the best meal of your life. You never learn who the guest who burned was. But you have the feeling, ever after, that somewhere in the south someone counts you as a guest of the house.

choices.text: Sit in the empty seat

ok.log: You sit down on the scorched cushion. Somebody gasps. The bird looks at you for a long, hot moment, and then laughs, a great crackling laugh that sets the tablecloth smouldering at one end. "Brave," it says. "Or rude. In the south it is often the same thing." It fills your cup itself, with tea, because you asked. All through the meal the seat is warm under you, very warm, and when you rise at sunset it has left a faint red print on your robe that never washes out.

fail.log: You sit down on the scorched cushion and it is hot, hot as a stove lid, and you jump up again with a yelp that the whole table hears. The bird laughs so hard that a dish of peaches catches fire. "Rude," it says, still laughing, "and now you know why the seat is empty." It finds you another cushion, and pours your tea itself, and is very kind to you for the rest of the meal, which is somehow worse. (-6 health)

choices.text: Do as the south does: sing for your place at the table

effects.log: You stand and sing for your place, the way they do at southern banquets: an old harvest song from your own village, a bit off-key, with the verse about the drunk uncle in it. Halfway through, the bird begins to sing too, under you, a harmony like heat rising off a summer road, and the guests clap the beat on the table. When you sit down the bird says, "Now you are a guest," and gives you the seat beside its own wing. You remember the harmony all your life and can never quite hum it.

events.text: Years after the banquet in the Southern Palace, an invitation comes to your door in heaven: a sheet of red paper, slightly scorched at the edges, in a looping hand that seems to have been written with a feather. It says only: "The table is set again. Your seat is kept."

choices.text: Go, and bring a dish from your own home below

effects.log: You bring a pot of the plain bean-paste stew of the village you came from, the one place below you still dream of. The bird eats three bowls of it, very fast, with its eyes closed, and then is quiet for a while. "Nobody brings me food," it says at last. "They bring me songs, and complaints, and records to sign." The next year there is a second pot of stew in the Southern Palace, made by its cooks, not quite right. You go and fix it.

choices.text: Write back that you will come when the seat of the burned guest is filled

effects.log: You write it on the back of the red paper and send it back with the messenger. A year passes. Then another invitation comes, and in the margin, in the same looping hand: "Filled. Come and see who." You go. In the scorched seat sits an old, thin, quiet immortal you have never met, who once, they tell you, set the south on fire in anger, and was forgiven at this table. You toast them. They cry.

events.text: Since the coldest night, the fire in the jar has been different. It never goes out, however badly you bank it. On frosty mornings it is already up before you are. And sometimes, when the house is quiet, the fire chirps. This morning an aunt of the house heard it, and stopped with the rice scoop in her hand, and looked at you.

choices.text: Say it is the green pine popping

effects.log: "Green pine," you say. "It pops." The aunt looks at the jar, and at you, and at the pine needles you keep in a bundle by it, and says "Hm." But that evening she leaves a pinch of rice on the edge of the stove shelf beside the water bowl, and in the morning it is gone, and you both pretend not to notice.

choices.text: Tell her the truth, all of it

effects.log: You tell her. She sits down on the kitchen step and laughs until she has to wipe her eyes. "My grandmother said it," she says. "She said the fire in this house was never just a fire. Nobody believed her either." From then on the two of you keep it together, and every winter the coldest night is the warmest one in the house.

choices.text: Feed it a pine needle, there and then, so she sees

effects.log: You kneel and lay a pine needle on the ash. The fire leans up to take it, the way a chick reaches for a seed. The aunt drops the rice scoop. Then she kneels down beside you, slowly, and lays a pine needle on the ash herself, and the fire takes that one too, and chirps, and she puts her hand over her mouth.

events.text: Someone new has married into the house this spring, and now the keeping of the fire is theirs. Every morning for a week they have found the jar dead cold, and every morning someone has had to run for fire, and the house is muttering. The newcomer is in tears. You have a fair idea what is happening, because the ash every morning has tiny three-toed prints in it.

choices.text: Sit up all night with the newcomer and watch

effects.log: You sit up together in the dark kitchen. At the hour of the ox, the embers in the jar begin to vanish, one by one, as if something were eating them. Then a small red bird climbs out of the ash, round as a dumpling, and goes to sleep on the warm stove shelf. The newcomer stares. "It is growing," you whisper. "It eats the embers. It always came back." In the morning you show the household the prints. Nobody blames the newcomer again.

choices.text: Chase it out with a stick, the way the old story says

ok.log: You wait with a stick, and when the red thing climbs out of the ash you go after it, out of the kitchen, across the yard, over the wall and up the hill in the dark, until it vanishes into a hollow under an old pine. You dig there at dawn, as the story says to, and find not gold but a wild root, old and forked, that a medicine dealer pays fifteen taels for. When you come home the jar is lit, and chirping, as if nothing had happened.

fail.log: You chase it over the wall and up the hill in the dark and fall in the stream. When you limp home, wet to the waist, the jar is lit and warm and the little red bird is asleep on the stove shelf again, and the newcomer is sitting beside it, laughing at you. (-4 health)

choices.text: Tell the newcomer the story of the coldest night

effects.log: You tell the whole story, in a whisper, by the jar. The newcomer listens with wide eyes. That night they lay a pine needle on the ash before they go to bed. In the morning the jar is lit. It is lit every morning after that, and the newcomer keeps it for years, and is the one, in the end, who tells the story to the children.

events.text: You are old, and it is time to hand the fire jar on. The youngest of the house is eight, and solemn, and has been told this is a great honour. The fire in the jar has not chirped in years. It went away, you think, a long time ago, to do whatever red birds grow up to do. Tonight, as you set the jar in the child's arms, a warm wind comes in under the door from the south, in winter.

choices.text: Tell the child about the pine needle

effects.log: "Every night," you say, "one pine needle. Just in case." The child nods hard. At the door a red glow passes over the yard, high up, quick, like a shooting star going the wrong way, and in the jar the fire leaps once, and chirps. The child shrieks with joy. You sit down on the kitchen step, because your knees have gone, and you laugh.

choices.text: Say nothing about birds; let the child find out

effects.log: You say only: keep it well. The child keeps it well. Years later, after you are gone, you hope, the child wakes on a coldest night to a cold jar and a red point in the ash that blinks. That is how it should be found. Not told. You go to sleep that night smelling pine smoke, and dream of a red bird on a ridge-pole, much bigger than you remember, bowing.

events.text: The burn on your palm from the coldest night has healed into a round red mark. It is a strange mark. In winter it is warm. Near a cooking fire it itches. And tonight, on a mountain path in snow, with the tinder wet and the light going, you hold your hand over the dead campfire, without thinking, and the ash under it begins to smoke.

choices.text: Hold it there and see what happens

effects.log: You hold it. The smoke thickens, and a red point appears in the ash under your palm, and then a small flame, and then a fire, enough to cook on. Your palm does not hurt. It feels, in fact, as if someone were holding it from the other side. You eat hot rice in the snow and sleep warm and in the morning the mark is a little brighter.

choices.text: Snatch your hand back

effects.log: You snatch your hand back and the smoke stops at once. You sit in the dark and the cold, staring at your palm. Then, carefully, you hold it out again. The ash smokes. You laugh out loud, alone on the mountain, and have the best fire of your life, and tell nobody, ever.

events.text: On a summer evening, on the veranda of an inn far from home, a red bird the size of a magpie lands on the rail beside you. Its feathers move like flame in a draught. It looks at your hand, the one with the scar, and puts its head on one side, the way a person does when they are not sure they remember a face.

choices.text: Hold out your palm

effects.log: You hold it out, scar up. The bird hops onto your fingers. It weighs nothing and it is hot as a teapot. It bends and touches its beak, once, to the middle of the scar, the way you might touch a door you used to live behind. Then it flies off into the dusk. The scar does not change. But you sleep, after that, the way you slept as a child.

choices.text: Say, quietly: you burned me

effects.log: "You burned me," you say, not angry. The bird ducks its head, quick, almost embarrassed, and then puffs up its feathers and looks away, the way a child does when it is sorry and will not say so. It sits beside you on the rail until the sun is down. In the morning there is a small red feather on your pillow, and it is warm.

events.text: The Pak house, who gave you the coal on the coldest night, have had nothing but luck since. Their sow has had twelve piglets. Their son passed the county examination. Their fire, they say, has not gone out once. The old woman of the house says, with great bitterness, that the luck of your house walked over the wall in a pot.

choices.text: Go to the Paks and ask for a coal back

effects.log: Old Pak laughs, and gives you a coal in a pot, and walks back with you to see it put in your jar. The coal goes in, and the fire in your jar leaps, and chirps. Old Pak goes white and then grins. "Half each," he says, "like good neighbours." The two houses share a fire from then on, back and forth over the wall, every New Year. Grandmother is not entirely satisfied, but she eats the Paks' rice cakes.

choices.text: Tell grandmother luck is not a coal

effects.log: "Luck is not a coal," you say. Grandmother says that is exactly what a young fool would say. But that winter, when the Paks' roof falls in under the snow, it is your house they come to, and your fire that warms them, and old Pak and the old woman of the house sit by it together all season, quarrelling happily about whose fire it really is.

events.text: A fire breaks out at the end of the lane at midday, in a high wind, and runs along the thatch from roof to roof. It is coming toward your house and the Paks' together. As the whole lane runs with buckets, you see, in the smoke above the two houses, something red and quick going back and forth, back and forth, like a sheepdog.

choices.text: Fight the fire beside it

ok.log: You get up on the Paks' roof with a wet straw mat and beat at the sparks, and every spark you miss, something red catches in the air and swallows. The fire stops at the wall between the two houses, as if at a line. Seven houses down the lane are gone. Yours and the Paks' have not one scorched straw. The lane says you are a hero. You know who the hero was.

fail.log: You get up on the roof and the smoke takes you and you fall off into the yard. When you can see again, the fire has stopped at the wall between your house and the Paks', exactly, and a small red bird is sitting on the wall, looking at you with what is clearly amusement. (-8 health)

choices.text: Get the old people and children out first

effects.log: You leave the roofs to the red thing and go house to house getting the old and the small out into the paddies. When you come back with the last grandmother on your back, the fire has stopped at the wall between your house and the Paks', and the red thing is gone, and nobody was hurt. The lane rebuilds. Every house in it, the next New Year, borrows a coal from yours.

events.text: Every first full moon since the year of the widow Seo's roof, you have looked for the red bird over the dykes when the fire cans are swinging. This year a boy from the next house, who has sworn to catch it, has made a net of hemp on a long pole and is waiting on the dyke with it.

choices.text: Warn the bird: swing your can in a wide slow circle away from the boy

effects.log: You swing your can wide and slow, away from the net, toward the far paddies, round and round like a beacon. A small red spark comes down out of the dark, circles your can once, and goes off low over the far paddies, nowhere near the boy, who swings at nothing all night. In the morning there is a single red feather on your doorstep, warm.

choices.text: Help the boy: you want to see it close too

ok.log: You help, and the net comes down over something red, and for one moment you are looking at it close: a bird the size of a fist, furious, every feather like a flame, eyes like two coals. Then the hemp net goes up in a puff of smoke and the bird is gone and the boy is sitting in the paddy holding a burnt pole. You are both perfectly happy about it for the rest of your lives.

fail.log: You help, and the net swings, and catches you across the face. The boy falls in the paddy. Somewhere above you something small and red laughs, a crackle like dry sticks. (-3 health)

choices.text: Tell the boy to leave it be

effects.log: "Leave it be," you say. "It saved Seo's roof." The boy argues, and then sulks, and then, very late, when the cans are almost out, says that if it saved Seo's roof he supposes it can stay. He puts down the net. A spark comes down out of the sky and sits on the end of the pole for a moment, as if to make a point, and goes.

events.text: You are grown, and this year you are the one tying the strings on the children's fire cans and telling them to swing them away from the thatch. One of them, a small fierce child, asks you if it is true about the red bird. All the children go quiet to hear.

choices.text: Tell them it is true, and to swing their cans carefully for it

effects.log: "True," you say. "Swing them carefully. It likes a good wide circle." The children swing them very carefully, all night, in wide circles. Nothing catches. Very late, when they are tired, a red spark comes down among the swinging cans and goes round and round with them, in and out, like a child playing. Every one of them sees it.

choices.text: Say: maybe; keep your eyes on your string

effects.log: "Maybe," you say. "Eyes on your string." The fierce child glares at you all night. But at midnight one string snaps, and a can goes sailing toward the widow Seo's grandson's roof, and something red catches it in the air and puts it down on the ice. The fierce child turns round and looks at you. You shrug, very slightly.

events.text: The commander of the coast has made you captain of the beacon hill: five chimneys, ten soldiers, and a hut that leaks. One fire every evening, all is well. And every evening, now, when you light it, a red bird comes from somewhere south and sits on the rim of the first chimney with its feathers fluffed, warming itself in the smoke, and watches the sea with you until dark.
events.arc: The Captain of the Beacon Hill

choices.text: Leave a bowl of grilled fish on the hut roof for it

effects.log: You leave grilled mackerel on the roof. In the morning the bowl is licked clean and set neatly upside down. The soldiers think you are mad. But in the fog season, when nobody can see the next hill, the red bird flies the signal there itself, a red streak through the white, and the next hill lights its one fire, and the soldiers stop thinking you are mad.

choices.text: Ask it, out loud, what it sees out there

effects.log: "What do you see?" you ask, feeling foolish. The bird turns one burning eye on you, and then looks back out at the sea, and its feathers tighten, and it stares hard at one place on the horizon. You look where it looks. Nothing. You double the watch that night anyway. At dawn three pirate ships come round the headland exactly there, into a coast that is ready for them.

choices.text: Drill the soldiers harder: a bird is not a sentry

effects.log: You drill them until they can light five chimneys in the dark in the time it takes to say it. The bird watches the drill from the chimney rim, head on one side, and on the third night it hops down and walks along the row of soldiers like an inspecting officer. The soldiers stand very straight. So, you notice, do you.

events.text: A dusk in early summer. Sails on the horizon, many, in a long line, not fishing boats. Your hands are already reaching for the brand. And the red bird, which has sat on your first chimney every evening for years, is not there. For the first time, you must count the sails alone.
events.arc: The Captain of the Beacon Hill

choices.text: Count them yourself, and light what you truly see

ok.log: You count. Twenty-two sails, war rig, heading for the river mouth. Three fires: near the shore. Your soldiers light them in the time it takes to say it. The next hill answers three, and the next, and the coast is ready. Long after dark, when the danger is past, a red shape comes down out of the night and sits on the first chimney, shaking rain off its feathers. It was watching from the next hill all along, you realise. Seeing whether you could.

fail.log: You count wrong: you light two, and they are closer than you thought. The raiders make the beach before the soldiers do. You are down on the sand with a spear all night, and it is a near thing. In the morning the red bird is on the first chimney again. It does not look at you as if you failed. It looks at you as if you will count better next time. (-6 health)

choices.text: Light five at once: better too many than too few

effects.log: Five. The coast empties into the hills. It turns out to have been three: near the shore, not battle. The commander is not pleased, but nobody died. When the red bird comes back that night it sits on the chimney with its back to you for a long time. Then, slowly, it turns round. You have the feeling you have been forgiven, and also that you will be expected to count next time.

events.text: You are old, and leaving the beacon hill to a younger captain, a nervous one who has never seen a raid. On your last evening you light the one fire together. The red bird comes down out of the south as it always does, but it is bigger now, much bigger, the size of a crane, and its tail trails sparks down the whole hillside.
events.arc: The Captain of the Beacon Hill

choices.text: Introduce the new captain to it, properly, with a bow

effects.log: You bow to the bird and say the new captain's name, and their family's, and their village. The new captain, white as rice, bows too. The great bird bows back. Then it leans down and looks at the new captain for a long time, close, as if memorising a face. When you walk down the hill for the last time, you look back. Two figures on the hill, and one fire, and above it a red shape settling onto the chimney rim to watch the sea.

choices.text: Tell the new captain to count the sails alone

effects.log: "It will not always come," you say. "Count them yourself. Light what you see." The new captain nods, very serious. The bird, listening on the chimney, ruffles its feathers in what you are almost sure is approval. You walk down the hill and do not look back. You do not need to.

events.text: Your back has healed from the flogging for the five fires. It was a fishing fleet. The coast emptied for three days. An old fisherwoman lost her winter stores to looters while she hid in the hills, and she has come to the beacon hill to tell you so to your face.

choices.text: Listen to all of it, and say you are sorry

effects.log: You listen to all of it. It takes a long time. When she is finished you say you are sorry, and that you will make it good. She snorts. But you spend the whole winter carrying her fish to market on your days off, and mending her nets, and by spring she has started calling you the beacon fool, which on that coast is nearly affectionate.

choices.text: Tell her a red bird lit the fires

effects.log: "A red bird lit them," you say. She stares at you. Then she laughs until she has to sit down on a chimney. "Of course it did," she says. "The bird of the south. Everybody's grandmother saw it once." She goes away shaking her head. But at the market, months later, you hear her telling it, and in her telling the bird was magnificent and you were a fool, which is about right.

choices.text: Say the capital needed to hear, and it heard

effects.log: "The capital heard," you say. "Next time it will listen faster." She looks at you with real contempt. "The capital," she says, "is not the one that starves." You think about that for a very long time. Years. It is the most useful thing anyone ever says to you.

events.text: Years later, you are an officer on another coast, and a young beacon soldier has been brought before you for lighting four fires for a whale. The coast emptied. The rules say a flogging. The soldier says, shaking, that the wood would not light and then it did, all at once, and something red was in the smoke.

choices.text: Spare the flogging and give them your own story

effects.log: You send everyone out and tell the soldier about the rain, the sails, the five fires and the flogging and the old fisherwoman. The soldier listens, wide-eyed. "So what do I do," they ask, "when the wood lights by itself?" "Count," you say. "It lights. You count." You report the whale as a training exercise. Nobody believes it. Nobody presses it either.

choices.text: Let the flogging stand, and stand beside them through it

effects.log: The rule stands. But you stand beside the soldier through every stroke, and afterwards you carry them to the hut yourself, and sit with them, and tell them about your own back. On the rim of the beacon chimney outside, in the dusk, something red sits watching, and does not leave until the soldier is asleep.

events.text: The village that burned the night you lit one fire was called Saetgol. Eleven houses. The pirates took the rice and the boats and set the rest alight, and four people died in it. Nobody blames you. Nobody knows. There was one fire on your hill that night, and one fire was the rule when you were not sure. You go down to Saetgol on your first day off.

choices.text: Stay, and help them rebuild

effects.log: You stay all your leave and the next, cutting timber, raising beams, re-thatching. The survivors think you are a strange soldier, and feed you, and stop asking why. When the last roof is on, an old man asks your name so the village can remember who helped. You tell him. You do not tell him the rest. That night the first fire of the new Saetgol is lit, and the smoke goes straight up, and very high in it something red is circling.

choices.text: Tell the headman what you did

effects.log: You tell the headman everything. He listens without moving. Then he says: "You lit one because you were not sure. My brother lit no lantern on his boat once because he was not sure, and a ship ran him down." A long pause. "Come back and help us with the boats." You do. For years.

choices.text: Leave money at the shrine and go, because you cannot face them

effects.log: You leave five taels at the village shrine and walk away fast. It is not enough and you know it. That night on your hill you dream of the red bird flying away south into the rain, and you wake up knowing you will go back. It takes you two years. But you go back.

events.text: Pirates again, at dusk, off the same coast. You are no longer a beacon soldier. You are a martial artist with a reputation, and you happen to be in Saetgol, the rebuilt village, eating fish soup, when the sails come round the headland. On the hill above, the beacon post lights two fires: an enemy sighted. Somebody up there counted right.

choices.text: Hold the beach while the village runs

ok.log: You hold the beach. You do not remember most of it: the boats grinding on the sand, the first rush, the captain with the hooked blade. You remember the end, when the last of them shove off, and you turn round and the whole of Saetgol is standing on the dyke behind you, alive, every one. And above the beacon hill, in the last of the light, something red and huge is circling, round and round, like a bird over a nest it has decided to keep.

fail.log: You hold the beach until you cannot. The captain's hooked blade knocks you down in the surf. But the village is up in the hills by then, every one, and the soldiers from the beacon post are coming down the slope. You wake in an old woman's house in Saetgol with your side bound up. She tells you, sternly, that a red bird sat on her roof all night. (-16 health)

choices.text: Get the children and the old people up the hill first

effects.log: You carry the old and herd the small up the hill path to the beacon post, two at a time, three, until the village is empty and the soldiers are on the beach. The pirates find nothing but fish soup and burn nothing, because the wind, which has been from the sea all day, suddenly and very strangely blows from the land, and their torches gutter. Saetgol stands. You are sitting on the beacon hill when it is over, shaking, with somebody's grandchild asleep in your lap.

events.text: Word has gone round the medicine markets of the south: a real vermilion feather was sold in the port, and the talismans written in it work. Now a quiet, well-dressed person with red-stained fingers has come to your sect gate, asking very politely to speak to the disciple who was in the dealer's shop that day. They say they are a dealer in pigments. They have a net folded very small in a bag at their belt.

choices.text: Tell them nothing, and send them away

effects.log: You tell them there is no such disciple. They smile, bow, and leave a card with an address in the capital, in case you remember. You burn the card. That night you dream of a red bird somewhere far south, sleeping in the warm ash of a kiln, and of a net, very fine, drawing closer. You wake sweating and do not know who to warn.

choices.text: Ask them what they want it for

effects.log: "Ink," the dealer says simply. "There is no red like it. A talisman written in it does not wear out. A thousand of them could make a province safe from every hungry ghost in it." A pause. "And there is a bird somewhere that grows them. Think of how many could be written in a whole bird." They smile, and bow, and go. You sit for a long time with your hands cold.

choices.text: Follow them, quietly, to see where they go

ok.log: You follow them through three towns to a house by the southern sea with a red-stained courtyard, mortars along the wall, and nets drying on poles: very fine nets, of a kind of silk that does not burn. You write down the address. You do not yet know what you will do with it. But now you know where the cinnabar hunters live.

fail.log: You follow them two towns, and in the third they are waiting for you round a corner, quite pleasant, and tell you that following people is rude, and that a disciple who knows where a red bird sleeps would be very valuable to them. You get away. Your wrist is sprained. You do not know where the bird sleeps, and you are very glad. (-4 health)

events.text: A red bird the size of a hawk lands on the wall of your courtyard at dusk, in summer, and looks at you. You know the colour of its tail. One feather in the long fan of it is new, shorter than the rest, still growing in.

choices.text: Bow, and say where the feather went

effects.log: You bow, and tell it, plainly: the dealer, the box, what became of it, and the people with the nets. The bird listens with its head down. When you are done it lifts its head and looks south, toward the sea, a long time. Then it flies. You do not know whether you have warned it or hurt it. You hope you have warned it.

choices.text: Hold out something of your own in exchange

effects.log: You take the best thing you own, a small worn charm you have carried since you were small, and hold it out on your palm. The bird looks at it, and at you, and then very gently takes it in its beak, and sets it down again on the wall beside you, and nudges it back toward your hand. It is not a trade, it seems to say. Then it is gone. On the wall where it stood the stone is warm until morning.

events.text: Since the banquet on the southern peak, summer treats you as a guest. The heat of the dog days does not tire you. Fires you light catch at once. Other martial artists notice: at a gathering of masters, an old fire-art master from the south looks at you across the courtyard and comes straight over, and asks, very low, "Whose table did you eat at?"

choices.text: Tell the master the truth

effects.log: You tell it. The master listens, and goes pale, and then bows to you, a deep formal bow, the kind for a senior. "Sixty years I have practised fire," the master says. "I have never been asked to that table. Tell me one thing: was the empty seat still empty?" You tell them. They go away thinking hard.

choices.text: Say you ate at a table in the south, and leave it there

effects.log: "A table in the south," you say. The master laughs. "So did we all," the master says, "once, in a dream." But at the end of the gathering they press a small packet into your hand: dried apricot and jujube wood, the woods of summer's new fire, tied with red thread. "For a guest," they say. "Guests bring wood."

events.text: On the summer solstice, years after the banquet, at noon, the sky to the south goes red again. Not for you. Over a valley far off, the seven groups of stars are coming down together to someone else's table. You can see the long table from your peak, tiny, and a figure standing beside the scorched seat, not knowing what to do.

choices.text: Raise your cup from where you stand

effects.log: You lift your cup toward the far table and drink. Far off, the figure by the scorched seat looks up, as if they had heard something, and then, slowly, lifts their own cup to the empty seat. The great bird bows. You laugh out loud on your peak, alone, and the heat of the noon sun is like a hand on your back.

choices.text: Go down there and sit beside them, as one guest to another

effects.log: You go. It takes you until the meal is half over. The bird sees you coming and laughs its crackling laugh and has a cushion brought, and you sit beside the new guest and tell them, quietly, which dish to try first and which song the bird likes. When you leave at sunset you are fairly sure you have just done what someone did for you, once, without your noticing.

events.text: Early summer, and the magistrate's runners have come up the valley road with clay pots of new fire, rubbed at the county office from apricot and jujube wood, the woods of summer. Old fire, the runners say, kept too long grows fierce, and sickness follows. By order every house must put out its old fire today and take the new. The old woman next door is sitting on her kitchen step with her arms round her fire jar, and will not move.

choices.text: Help the runners: it is the law, and it is for the sickness

effects.log: You help carry the pots house to house. At the old woman's door you kneel and tell her, gently, that her fire will not be lost, only made young. She lets you take the jar. When you tip the old ashes out, something small and red skips out of them, across the yard, and straight into the runner's pot of new fire, where it sits looking pleased. The runner does not notice. You do.

choices.text: Sit down on the step beside the old woman

effects.log: You sit down beside her. The runners argue, and then shrug, and go on to the next house, and promise to come back. The old woman tells you her fire was lit by her mother-in-law's mother-in-law. At dusk she takes one coal from her old jar and drops it into the new fire the runners left by the gate, and only then pours water on the rest. "There," she says. "Now it is both."

choices.text: Ask the runner how the new fire is made

effects.log: The runner, pleased to be asked, squats in the dust and shows you: a bow, a spindle of jujube, a block of apricot, sawing back and forth until the wood smokes and a black dust gathers and glows. "Spring is elm and willow," the runner says. "Summer, apricot and jujube. Autumn, oak. Winter, birch. Every season its own wood, so the fire is the season's." You try it and blister your hands and get a spark on the fortieth try.

events.text: A summer of fevers in the next village. The old people there say it is because the headman's house never changed its fire, not in fifty years: too proud, they say, of an old fire. The headman's house is the worst of all. Coughs, quarrels, a child scalded, a barn burned. Their old fire, people whisper, has gone fierce.

choices.text: Carry them new fire from your own village, of the summer's wood

effects.log: You carry a pot of new fire over the hill at dawn, apricot and jujube, wrapped in wet straw. The headman's old wife takes it in shaking hands. The old fire is put out with a great hiss and a stink and, you would swear, an angry crackle. Within a month the fevers in that house go down. The headman sends you a sack of rice and an apology for something he does not name.

choices.text: Go and look at the old fire yourself

ok.log: You kneel by the headman's hearth. The fire in it is the wrong colour, too white at the heart, and it roars when nobody feeds it, and the air around it is dry as a kiln. It is not wicked. It is old, and too hot, and nobody has been looking after it. You put it out yourself, carefully, and lay new fire, and the house sighs like a person setting down a load.

fail.log: You kneel by the headman's hearth and the old fire spits a coal into your sleeve. You beat it out and burn your arm. The headman's house is changed in the end by the magistrate's runners, by order, and the fevers go down. You keep the burn mark as a lesson about old fires. (-4 health)

events.text: It is your house's turn to bring new fire to the village this summer. You have the bow and the jujube spindle and the block of apricot wood, and the whole village waiting in the yard. You saw and saw. Nothing. The wood is damp. The headman clears his throat. On the ridge of your roof, very quietly, a small red bird has landed.

choices.text: Keep sawing, and do not look up

effects.log: You keep sawing and do not look at the roof. The wood smokes, and smokes, and then all at once glows, far too bright, and catches, and the yard cheers. You do not look up until everyone has carried their fire home. When you do, the ridge is empty, and there is one tiny scorch mark on the tile.

choices.text: Look up and say: help, please

effects.log: "Please," you say, out loud, to your own roof, in front of the whole village. A pause. Then something red drops off the ridge like a falling ember, straight into your tinder, and the tinder bursts into flame, and the bird is up and gone before most of them have seen anything at all. The headman, who saw, says nothing for a whole year, and then, at New Year, bows to your roof.

events.text: The longest night of the year, and the red-bean porridge is ready, thick and dark red, with sticky rice balls in it for each year of your age. Before anyone eats, the grandmother of the house sends you out with a bowl to fling it on the gate and the walls and the well, because red drives the ghosts away on the longest night. As you fling the first spoonful at the gate, a small red bird lands on the gatepost, and the porridge hits it squarely.

choices.text: Apologise to it, and wipe it off with your sleeve

effects.log: You put the bowl down and wipe its feathers clean with the end of your sleeve, apologising. It submits with enormous dignity. Then it hops down, eats one rice ball out of your bowl, and flies off. Grandmother, watching from the door, says a red bird on the longest night is the best omen she ever heard of, and makes you sit nearest the stove.

choices.text: Fling a second spoonful, laughing

effects.log: You fling another, laughing, and miss, and the bird ducks and puffs up its feathers and glares at you like a tiny furious official. Then it hops into the porridge on the gatepost and starts eating it. Grandmother laughs so hard she has to sit down in the snow.

choices.text: Ask grandmother why red drives off ghosts

effects.log: "Red is the yang colour," Grandmother says. "Fire, summer, the south, noon. Ghosts are yin: cold, dark, the north, midnight. On the longest night the yin is strongest, so we put red on the gate." She looks at the bird on the gatepost, eating porridge. "Some years," she says, "the south sends its own."

events.text: Another longest night. A plague has gone through the county this winter, and every gate in the village is red with porridge, thick, desperate. Your bowl is the last in the house: there is not enough for the gate and for supper too.

choices.text: Put it on the gate

effects.log: You fling it on the gate and go hungry. In the night, you hear it: something small hopping along the top of the wall, round and round the whole house, like a watchman. In the morning there is not a ghost in the county that came near your gate, and the sick in your house are better. Your stomach is very empty and you do not mind.

choices.text: Feed the house, and put one spoonful on the gate

effects.log: You feed everyone and save one spoonful for the gate, and fling it, and say to the dark, "It is all we have." In the morning the one spoonful has been eaten off the gate, very neatly, and on the gatepost, frozen into the frost, are three tiny prints, and the whole house is well.

events.text: The hardest week of winter. The widow at the end of the lane has no wood and no rice and is too proud to ask. You have been leaving a bundle of sticks at her door at night, but you have none left. Tonight, going past, you see light through her kitchen door. Her stove is lit, burning steady, and the widow is kneeling in front of it with her hands over her mouth. There is no wood in it at all.

choices.text: Go in, and sit with her by it

effects.log: You go in and sit with her. The fire burns all night on nothing. Neither of you says a word about it. Toward dawn something small and red comes out of the firebox, hops up onto the stove shelf beside the water bowl, and goes to sleep with its head under its wing. The widow covers it with the corner of a clean cloth. The fire keeps burning.

choices.text: Run for rice, so there is something to cook on it

effects.log: You run home and steal a bowl of rice from your own kitchen and run back. The widow cooks it on the fire that burns on nothing, and eats, crying, and makes you eat half. In the morning the fire is a little lower, as if tired. You and three neighbours go up the mountain for wood that day, because a fire that has done that much should not have to do it all.

events.text: The widow at the end of the lane has not been cold one day in the years since the night her stove lit itself. Her house is the warmest in the village; children go there to thaw their hands; travellers knock. She is old now, and has asked you to come, because she is dying, and wants to tell someone what to do with the fire.

choices.text: Promise to keep it yourself

effects.log: "Keep it," she says, "and keep the water bowl full, and one pine needle a night." You promise. She dies easy, in a warm room. The fire in her stove, as they carry her out, burns very low, and very red, and makes a sound that nobody but you knows is a bird grieving. You carry a coal of it home in a pot, and it never goes out.

choices.text: Ask her who she thinks lit it

effects.log: "The south," she says. "My mother said the south remembers cold kitchens." She smiles. "I left it grilled fish heads every New Year. It ate them." She dies that night. The fire goes on burning in her empty house all winter, with no one feeding it, and the village children still go there to warm their hands.

events.text: A swallow chick has fallen out of the nest under your eaves and broken its leg. It lies in the dust of the yard, beak open. Everybody knows the story: the kind brother who mended a swallow's leg, and the gourd seed it brought him in the spring, and the treasure. Everybody also knows about the cruel brother.

choices.text: Bind the leg with thread and put it back in the nest

effects.log: You splint it with a sliver of bamboo and white thread, the way you have seen the bonesetter do, and climb up and put it back in the nest. It lives. In autumn the swallows go south with the rest, and the bound one is last to leave, and circles your roof twice. On the ridge, watching them go, sits a red bird you have never seen before, which flies south with them.

choices.text: Bind it, and ask for nothing

effects.log: You bind it and say to it, firmly, out loud, that you do not want a gourd seed, thank you, and it is just a leg. A small neighbour laughs at you. But it seems important. In autumn the swallows go, and the bound one goes with them, and you are glad.

events.text: The third day of the third month: the swallows come back from the warm country, the day the old people say they always come back. The bound one is with them, a grown bird now, and it drops something into your hands as it passes, and goes up to its old nest. In your palm is a seed, flat and pale. A gourd seed. Flying low over the roof behind the swallows is a small red bird, which seems to be making sure.

choices.text: Plant it by the wall

effects.log: You plant it. The vine climbs the wall and the roof faster than any gourd you ever saw, and in autumn there are three great gourds. You split the first open with half the lane watching. Inside: rice. Not gold, not silk: rice, good white rice, enough for the winter. The second: seed for the spring. The third you leave on the roof, unopened, because you have enough. Something about that feels right.

choices.text: Give it to the poorest house in the village

effects.log: You give it to the poorest house, the one with the five children and the sick father. They plant it. In autumn the gourds are full of rice. They never know where the seed came from. Watching them carry it in, you see the red bird on their roof ridge, looking at you, with its head on one side, as if you had done something it had not expected, and liked.

events.text: The rich man of the village heard about your gourd. This spring he has gone round every house with swallows under the eaves, and tonight you catch his servant on a ladder under your neighbour's eaves, with a stick, reaching for a nest. Everyone knows what the cruel brother in the story did.

choices.text: Pull the servant down off the ladder

ok.log: You pull the ladder out and the servant lands in the manure heap. The nest is safe. The rich man complains to the headman, who listens to the whole story and laughs in his face. That autumn the rich man plants a gourd seed he bought from a peddler, and it grows, and the gourds are full of hornets. Nobody in the village is surprised.

fail.log: You pull at the ladder and the servant kicks you in the face. But the noise wakes the whole lane, and the servant runs, and the nest is safe. You have a black eye for a week. A red bird sits on the eaves above the nest every night that week, and the servant does not come back. (-4 health)

choices.text: Tell the servant how the story ends

effects.log: "You know how the story ends," you say up the ladder. "The second brother's gourds were full of goblins." The servant stops with the stick in the air. Comes down. "He told me to," the servant says miserably. "I know," you say. The servant goes back and tells the rich man there were no swallows. There were. Everyone in the lane quietly agrees there were not.

events.text: It is your job every morning to fill the white bowl on the clay shelf above the stove with fresh water from the well, for the hearth spirit. Nobody may curse in the kitchen or put their feet near the stove, because the hearth spirit tells heaven everything. This month, every morning, the bowl is half empty, and the water left in it is warm.
events.arc: The Bowl on the Stove Shelf

choices.text: Fill it to the brim, and say good morning to the stove

effects.log: You fill it to the brim and say good morning to the stove, out loud, feeling silly. Something in the firebox crackles back. From then on the bowl is half empty every morning and the stove lights at the first breath, and once, at dawn, you catch a small grey-and-red chick drinking from the rim of the bowl, tipping its head back like a hen.

choices.text: Watch the bowl all night

effects.log: You watch all night. At the hour of the tiger a little sooty shape climbs out of the stove onto the shelf and drinks, then sits beside the bowl like an old man at a wine table, grumbling to itself in crackles, and then a second shape, smaller and redder, climbs up and drinks too, and is grumbled at. You never tell anyone. You would not know how.

events.text: An uncle of the house came home drunk last night and kicked the stove and cursed in the kitchen, and this morning nothing will light. Not the stove, not the jar, not a lamp. The house is cold and everyone is frightened. The old people say the hearth spirit is offended, and will tell heaven, and the house will have a bad year.
events.arc: The Bowl on the Stove Shelf

choices.text: Make the uncle apologise to the stove

effects.log: It takes all morning. In the end the uncle kneels in front of the stove, red-faced, and apologises to it, in full, with everyone watching. The stove lights on the next breath, with a pop like somebody laughing. The uncle does not drink for a year, and every time he passes the kitchen door he bows to it.

choices.text: Fill the bowl, clean the kitchen, and ask politely

effects.log: You fill the water bowl fresh, sweep every corner, wipe the soot from the shelf, and ask, politely, for fire. A long sulky silence. Then a small red spark jumps from somewhere up in the rafters into the stove, as if somebody younger and less offended had decided to overrule somebody older. The stove lights. You bow to the rafters too, to be safe.

events.text: Your family's rice is nearly ripe, and you have been set to guard it from the sparrows with a bamboo clapper. They come in clouds. And this autumn, among the brown sparrows, there is one bright red one. It is not afraid of the clapper. It is not afraid of the scarecrow. It is sitting on the scarecrow's straw hat, and the straw hat has begun to smoke.

choices.text: Run with water

effects.log: You run with the dipper and douse the hat, and the red sparrow flies up chirping, offended, and lands on the next dyke. The hat is ruined. You make a new one. The red sparrow comes back every day after, and sits on the new hat, and the hat never smokes again, as if it had learned, and the brown sparrows never come near your paddy again either.

choices.text: Let it sit: it is keeping the other sparrows off

effects.log: You notice that since it came, not one brown sparrow has landed in your paddy. You let the hat smoke. It never quite catches. Your family's rice is the only rice in the valley with every grain still on it at harvest. The scarecrow ends the autumn black on top, like a scholar's hat, and the village calls it the magistrate.

events.text: A harvest festival, and the children of the village are burning the old scarecrows on a bonfire at the end of the paddies, with songs. Yours, the one with the black hat, goes on last. As it catches, something red flies up out of the fire, circles the bonfire three times, and lands on your shoulder. It is bigger than it used to be.

choices.text: Stand very still

effects.log: You stand very still. It is hot, through your jacket, but it does not burn. It sits on your shoulder through the whole last song, watching the fire, as if it were at a festival too. Then it flies. The children talk about it until spring. One of them asks you, seriously, if it hurt. You say no. It was like standing next to summer.

choices.text: Sing the harvest song to it

effects.log: You start the old harvest song, and the children join in, and the red bird on your shoulder puts its head back and sings too, a sound like a kettle and a flute at once. The bonfire leaps up to the sky. Old people come out of their houses to look. Later, in the village, it is told as the year the harvest fire sang.

events.text: The boy from the next house has done it: crept up on the red bird that sits on the Kims' wall in the evenings, and pulled out its tail feather, and run off waving it. The bird screamed like a kettle. Now the boy is dancing in the lane, because his straw sandals have caught fire, both of them, and he is trying to stamp them out and hold the feather up at the same time.

choices.text: Throw him in the ditch

effects.log: You shove him into the irrigation ditch. Hiss. He comes up soaked and furious with a scorched pair of sandals and the feather still in his fist, and the whole lane laughs at him. On the Kims' wall, the bird, short one tail feather, puffs up and looks at you with grim approval.

choices.text: Make him give the feather back

effects.log: You get the feather off him, which takes some doing, and carry it to the Kims' wall and hold it up. The bird looks at it a long time. Then it takes it in its beak, and drops it into your hands, and turns its back. "It means keep it," says the oldest Kim grandmother, "and do not let him have it." The feather is warm in your box for years.

choices.text: Laugh too hard to help

effects.log: You laugh until you fall over. So does the whole lane. The boy stamps out his sandals himself, scarlet with rage. The bird on the wall watches all of you, and then, very distinctly, makes a sound like laughing too, a dry crackle, and a dry leaf on the Kims' roof begins to smoke. Everyone stops laughing at once.

events.text: The boy who pulled the bird's tail feather is grown, and a fire-watchman in the county town, and very good at it: he says he can smell a fire before it starts. He has come to find you, because last night, on the watchtower, a red bird the size of a hawk landed on the rail beside him, and looked at him, and he wants to know what it wants.

choices.text: Tell him it wants an apology

effects.log: "An apology," you say. He goes red to the ears. That night he climbs the watchtower with a dish of grilled fish and says sorry, at length, to the empty rail. You hear it from the street, and so does half the town. In the morning the fish is gone, and a single tail feather, red, has been laid on the rail, and he keeps it in his watchman's cap for the rest of his life.

choices.text: Tell him it wants him to keep watching

effects.log: "It wants you to keep watching," you say. "You smell fires. So does it." He thinks about that. The next year there is a terrible dry spring, and three times he rings the bell before anyone else has seen smoke, and three times a red bird is circling above the place he rang for. The town gives him a medal. He gives it to you, for no reason he will explain.

events.text: The first full moon, and the village has built a moon house in the empty paddy: a tall cone of pine branches and straw, with a door facing the rising moon. Whoever sees the moon first gets a son, or a good year, or a wish, depending on which grandmother you ask. When the moon comes up the moon house is lit. At the top of the flames something red is dancing, round and round, as if the fire had grown a bird.

choices.text: Make a wish to it

effects.log: You make a wish to the dancing red thing, quietly, not the usual kind. It stops dancing for one moment at the top of the flames and looks straight down at you. Then it goes on. Your wish comes true in the autumn, in a small way, and you never tell anyone what it was.

choices.text: Dance too, with the other young people

effects.log: You join the ring of young people dancing round the fire with the farmers' band, gongs and drums, faster and faster. Up in the flames the red thing dances faster too, matching you. Nobody else seems to notice. The fire burns twice as long as any moon house anybody can remember, and the old people say it is going to be a very good year. It is.

events.text: A bad year: the village is too poor to build a moon house. No pine, no straw to spare, no one has the heart. On the night of the first full moon you go out alone to the empty paddy with one armful of branches, because somebody should.

choices.text: Build it small, and light it

effects.log: You build a moon house no taller than a child and light it. It burns up fast and small. Then, at the top, something red begins to dance, and the fire climbs, and climbs, far higher than the branches can carry it, a column of fire as tall as the old pine. The whole village comes out. The year that follows is not good. But it is better than anyone feared.

choices.text: Sit by it and wait for the moon

effects.log: You build it and sit by it without lighting it, and wait for the moon. When the moon comes up over the hill, the branches catch on their own, from the top down. You sit by your little fire all night. In the morning there is not even ash, just a ring of warm earth in the frozen paddy, the first place the spring shoots come up.

events.text: Winter rain on the southern road, no inn for twenty li, and your cloak soaked through. On the hillside above the road there is a long pottery kiln, cooling after a firing, and the mouth of the firebox is still warm. You crawl in. It is wonderful. You are nearly asleep when something in the warm ash at the back of the firebox, something with eyes, says very clearly: "This is my bed."

choices.text: Apologise, and offer to share

effects.log: "I beg your pardon," you say into the dark. "May I share it?" A long pause. Then a grudging rustle, and the eyes move over to one side, and the ash where you lie gets warmer. You sleep the best night of your journey next to something that snores like a kettle. In the morning a red bird the size of a dove walks out of the firebox ahead of you, shakes ash off itself, and flies off without a glance back.

choices.text: Draw your sword

ok.log: You get your sword out, which is difficult lying down in a firebox. The eyes regard you. Then the whole back of the kiln goes red hot and you leave very fast, sword in hand, unharmed, and sit in the rain. Through the mouth of the firebox you can hear something laughing at you. You laugh too, eventually. It is a very silly position.

fail.log: You try to draw your sword and the ash at the back of the kiln flares up white and you come out of the firebox with your eyebrows gone. You spend the night in the rain. In the morning, crossly, a red bird walks out of the kiln past you, dry and warm, and does not even look at you. (-5 health)

choices.text: Get out, and sleep in the rain

effects.log: You back out into the rain, mumbling an apology. It is a long cold night. Toward dawn, though, a warm draught comes out of the kiln mouth toward you, steady as a breath, and you sleep after all, curled against the kiln wall. You think you were being looked after, a little, by something that did not want to share.

events.text: You pass the kiln on the southern road again, years later. It is firing: smoke pouring from the chimney holes all along its back, the potter's family feeding pine in at the side ports, everyone black with soot and dead tired. The potter says it is the third firing this year, and the first two failed, and if this one fails they will lose the kiln.

choices.text: Stay and help feed the fire through the night

effects.log: You feed pine through the side ports all night with the potter's family, until your arms shake. Near dawn, through a spy hole, you see something red moving deep in the white-hot heart of the kiln, settling in among the pots like a hen on eggs. The firing is good. When they open the kiln two days later, every pot is the colour of deep clear water over green stones.

choices.text: Bow to the kiln and go on your way

effects.log: You bow to the kiln, which the potter thinks is very odd, and go on your way. A month later you hear the third firing was the best in the valley in a generation. You are not surprised. You remember who sleeps in that firebox.

events.text: The potter of the kiln on the southern road has died, and the family is selling the kiln to a rich merchant from the capital who wants to fire cheap bowls in great numbers, hot and fast, every week of the year. The family asks you, the traveller who helped them once, whether that is all right.

choices.text: Tell them to ask the kiln

effects.log: "Ask the kiln," you say. They think you are mad, but the grandmother of the house goes and kneels at the firebox mouth and asks. That night the kiln, cold for a month, glows red along its whole length on its own, and then goes dark. In the morning there is a crack down the middle of it. The merchant will not buy a cracked kiln. The family patches it themselves and fires it four times a year, slowly, as before.

choices.text: Help them bargain for a better price, and let it go

effects.log: You bargain the merchant up by half. The family is grateful. The kiln is fired every week after that, hot and fast. Within a year, you hear, it has cracked down its whole length, and nothing the merchant fires in it comes out whole. The merchant sells it back for less than he paid. The family fires it slowly, as before, and it works perfectly.

events.text: You have hired on for a winter with the charcoal burners in the oak forest: hard, black work, building the great mounds of oak logs under earth, lighting them, and keeping them for days at the edge of burning, never letting a flame break through. The old charcoal master says the whole art is patience. Tonight it is your watch, alone, and at one of the vents a red eye is looking out at you from inside the mound.

choices.text: Keep the watch as you were taught, and say nothing to it

effects.log: You watch the vents as you were taught: a little air here, a little earth there. The red eye watches you do it. All night, the mound burns perfectly, slow and even, no flame. In the morning the old master looks at the mound and then at you, and nods. The charcoal from that mound is the best of the winter. You did not do it alone, and you know it.

choices.text: Ask it, politely, to burn slow

effects.log: "Slow, please," you say to the vent. "The master says patience." The eye blinks. The mound goes, if anything, slower and steadier than you have ever seen one burn. In the morning the old master asks what you did. You say you asked it. The old master does not laugh. "My grandfather said that too," is all the master says.

events.text: A dry wind, and one of the charcoal mounds has broken open on the hillside: flames through the earth, sparks streaming into the dry oak leaves. The other burners are running with shovels. If it gets into the forest it will take the whole hill and the village below.

choices.text: Throw earth on it with everyone else

ok.log: You shovel earth until your hands bleed. At the worst moment, when the flames are into the leaves, something red streaks down out of the smoke and goes along the edge of the fire like a sheepdog along a flock, and the flames turn back from wherever it passes. You get the mound covered. The forest stands. The old master sits down in the ash and says nothing for a long time.

fail.log: You shovel until the smoke drops you. When you can breathe again it is out. The burners say the wind turned all at once, and the flames went back on themselves, and that a red bird was over the fire the whole time. You missed it, coughing in the leaves. (-8 health)

choices.text: Run down and warn the village

effects.log: You run down and get the village out with their cattle into the paddies. Looking back from the dykes, you see the fire on the hillside stop, and turn, and lie down, as if it had been told to. Something red circles above it twice and is gone. Not a house is touched. The headman insists you saved the village. You let him.

events.text: You are lodging in the capital with a family whose new daughter-in-law was told, on her first day, not to talk about anything she sees in the house. She has taken it to heart. Yesterday the kitchen caught fire and she put it out alone and said nothing at all, and was scolded: a fire, said her mother-in-law, is always worth mentioning. This evening, at dusk, she comes flying out onto the veranda, pointing at the southern hill above the city, where a single beacon fire has just been lit, and shouts "Fire! Fire!" at the top of her voice.

choices.text: Explain the beacon to her, kindly

effects.log: You explain: one fire on the southern hill every evening means all is well, and it comes all the way from the coast, hill to hill. She goes scarlet and then, to everyone's surprise, asks a great many sharp questions about how the counting works. By the end of the evening she knows more about the beacon roads than her husband does, and her mother-in-law is looking at her with new respect.

choices.text: Laugh until you cry

effects.log: You laugh until you cry, and so does half the lane, and so, after a frozen moment, does the mother-in-law, holding onto the gatepost. The bride stamps her foot. Then she laughs too. On the southern hill, in the beacon's one fire, you could swear something red is turning round and round in the flames, as if it had heard the joke.

choices.text: Look at the beacon properly: is it only one?

effects.log: You look properly, out of old habit. One fire. All is well. But above it, against the dark, a spark is circling the hill, round and round, too steady for a spark. You watch it for an hour, long after the family has gone in laughing. It never comes down. You decide the beacon of the southern hill has a watchman nobody pays.

events.text: Years later, on another dusk in the capital, the whole city goes still. On the southern hill, instead of one fire, there are two. And then, as people come running out into the lanes, three. The daughter-in-law who once shouted fire is a mother-in-law herself now, and is standing in her gate, counting, and she is the first to say it out loud: it is coming closer.

choices.text: Go to the Ministry of War and offer your sword

roll.foeName: The raiders on the coast road

ok.log: You go. The ministry, surprised, puts you with a cavalry troop riding south that night. It is a hard week on the coast road and you come back with a cut over your eye and your name in a report. The raid is turned back at the third beacon. When you come home, the woman who counted is at her gate, and tells you, crisply, that the southern hill showed one fire again on the sixth night, and she knew you were safe.

fail.log: You ride south with a cavalry troop and are hurt in the first skirmish and spend the war in a coast-town bed. The raid is turned back without you. The woman who counted sends you a jar of soup by the post road, with a note that one fire burns on the southern hill again, and that you are a fool. (-10 health)

choices.text: Help her get her family ready to leave

effects.log: You help her pack: the ancestral tablets first, then rice, then the children's winter clothes. You do not need to leave in the end: the fires drop back to two, then one, over three nights. But you will never forget the woman standing in her gate counting, calm as a general, while the whole city panicked round her.

events.text: You are passing through a fishing village on the southern coast when the beacon on the hill above lights two fires, and then three, and the villagers start running. Sails in the bay, close. Pirates. There is no garrison nearer than half a day.

choices.text: Hold the landing place

ok.log: You hold the landing place at the end of the jetty, where only two can come at you at once, and you hold it until the garrison comes over the hill at dawn. Your arms are dead and the jetty is a ruin. Not one house burned. On the beacon hill above, the three fires are burning very high, higher than wood alone should burn, all night.

fail.log: You hold the landing place until a club takes you behind the ear. The pirates get three houses and the rice store before the garrison comes. You wake up on a fisherman's floor. The fisherman's mother says the pirates did not stay long, because their own boats caught fire in the bay, all at once, nobody knows how. (-14 health)

choices.text: Get the village up the hill to the beacon post

effects.log: You herd the village up the hill to the beacon post, carrying the ones who cannot walk. From the hill you watch the pirates land and find an empty village. They loot, and set fire to the net-sheds, and the fire will not catch: every torch they throw goes out. They sail at midnight, swearing. In the morning the village comes down to a looted, unburned home.

events.text: The fishing village you defended has sent for you. The pirates are back, they say, but not at sea: their captain has come in by land, alone, unarmed, and is sitting in the village square asking to speak to whoever defended it. He says his ships keep catching fire, every time he sails along this coast, and he wants to know what you did.

choices.text: Tell him the coast has a guardian, and he should go home

effects.log: "The coast has a guardian," you say, "and it does not like you." The pirate captain looks at the beacon hill for a long time. "I believe it," he says. "I have seen it. Red, very big, over my mainmast." He goes. You hear he took his ships north, to colder coasts, and that his crews never stopped talking about the red bird of the south.

choices.text: Ask him why he raids

effects.log: He tells you: an island with no rice, a lord who takes half the fish, children. It does not make the burned villages right, and you tell him so. But you also tell him the fishing grounds to the west are empty and the coast towns there buy dried fish. He leaves without a word. Next year a ship comes to that coast to trade dried fish, and nothing on it catches fire.

events.text: The court has ordered a tribute vase from the kilns of the southwest coast, the jade-green ware the court calls kingfisher colour, and you have been hired to guard the kiln while it fires: forty hours, the potter {npc} says, without a break, and most firings fail. Two rival kilns would be glad to see this one fail. On the second night {npc} comes out from the spy hole grey in the face. "Something is in there," {npc} says. "In the fire. It is alive."

choices.text: Let it be: tell {npc} to keep firing

effects.log: "Keep firing," you say. {npc} stares at you, then at the kiln, and keeps firing. When the kiln is opened two days later every pot is perfect, and the tribute vase is a green so deep and clear the whole family goes silent looking at it. In the ash of the firebox there is one red feather. {npc} keeps it in the family shrine.

choices.text: Look through the spy hole yourself

effects.log: You put your eye to the spy hole. White heat, the pots glowing like lamps, and among them, settled in the hottest place with its wings half spread over the tribute vase like a hen over a chick, a bird made of the same white fire, looking back at you. You step away very carefully. "Keep firing," you tell {npc}. "Whatever happens. You have help."

choices.text: Guard the rival kilns' road instead: someone is coming

ok.log: You were right: a hired blade from a rival kiln comes up the hill at the hour of the ox with a bucket of seawater for the side ports. You meet them on the path. It is short. The firing goes on, and the vase comes out perfect, and {npc} never knows about the bucket, and the thing in the fire, you think, does.

fail.log: A hired blade from a rival kiln gets past you on the path, bleeding you as they go, and throws a bucket of seawater into a side port. The kiln hisses like a dragon. And then roars back up hotter than before, from the inside, as if something in there were very angry. The vase comes out perfect. {npc} binds your arm and asks no questions. (-9 health)

events.text: {npc} the potter has sent for you again. The court liked the tribute vase so much that it has ordered a hundred more by New Year. A hundred kingfisher pieces in one season is impossible, {npc} says; nobody has ever done it; and if the kiln fails, the court's officer will take the family's land instead.

choices.text: Help {npc} write to the court that it cannot be done

effects.log: You and {npc} write a careful letter: the clay, the firewood, the weather, one firing in five. The officer reads it, sneers, and then, unexpectedly, reads it again. The order comes back as twenty. {npc} fires slowly, all season, and the red thing in the fire comes every time, and twenty perfect pieces go to the capital. Nobody asks again.

choices.text: Stay and feed the kiln with {npc} all season
