effects.log: You stay. You feed pine through the side ports until your shoulders scream, firing after firing. Every firing, at the worst hour, the kiln goes white and steady from within. By New Year there are a hundred pieces, and not one cracked. {npc} weeps. In the ash of the last firing there is a red feather, and a little grey down, as if something very tired had moulted there.

events.text: {npc} the potter is very old and has asked you to come, because {npc} is going to fire the kiln one last time, and wants a witness. The grandchildren are feeding pine. {npc} sits by the firebox mouth with a cup of barley tea, talking to the fire, quite openly now, as to an old friend.

choices.text: Sit beside {npc} and listen

effects.log: You sit and listen. {npc} tells the fire about the family, the grandchildren, the clay pit, the price of rice. The fire crackles back. At dawn, {npc} falls asleep there, cup in hand, and does not wake. The firing is the best the kiln ever made. The grandchildren open it in silence. In the ash is a grey feather, and a red one, side by side.

choices.text: Ask the fire, for {npc}, whether it will stay with the family

effects.log: "Will you stay with them?" you ask the firebox, for {npc}, who is too proud to. The fire goes very still, and then flares once, high and white, and settles. {npc} laughs, delighted, like a child. "That is yes," {npc} says. "I know its yes." The grandchildren fire the kiln for years after, and it never fails them.

events.text: In a village forge on the southern road there is a fire that, people say, has not gone out in a hundred years, and anything forged in it holds an edge forever. You have brought your sword to be tempered there. The smith {npc} looks at the blade, and at you, and says: "The fire decides, not me. It does not like blades made for killing. Tell it what this one is for."
events.arc: The Forge That Does Not Go Out

choices.text: Tell the fire the truth about your sword

effects.log: You tell it the truth: who you have fought, who you have spared, who you would fight again. It takes a while. The fire listens, crackling. When you are done {npc} puts the blade in, and the fire takes it, and gives it back with a faint red line along the edge like a hairline of sunset. "It agreed with you," {npc} says. "Mostly."

choices.text: Tell the fire it is for protecting people

ok.log: "For protecting people," you say, and mean it. The fire takes the blade like a hand taking a hand. It comes out with a faint red line along the edge. {npc} raises an eyebrow. "It believed you," {npc} says. "See that you do too."

fail.log: "For protecting people," you say. The fire spits the blade back out onto the anvil, red hot, and a coal lands on your boot. {npc} sighs. "It does not care for speeches," {npc} says. "Come back when you know what the blade is for." You come back a year later. It takes the blade then. (-5 health)

choices.text: Ask {npc} who lit the fire

effects.log: "Nobody lit it," {npc} says. "A hundred years ago my great-great-grandparent's forge went cold in a famine, and in the morning there was a fire in it and a red bird on the anvil. That is the story. I have seen the bird twice. It sits on the bellows when the iron is good." {npc} tempers your blade. It comes out with a red line along the edge.

events.text: {npc} the smith has sent word: a lord's men have come to the forge with an order for five hundred spear-heads, for a war against the next province that everyone knows the lord started. They want them forged in the fire that does not go out. They have taken {npc}'s grandchild to the lord's house as surety.
events.arc: The Forge That Does Not Go Out

choices.text: Go and get the grandchild back

ok.log: You go into the lord's house by night and come out with the grandchild on your back and the steward's men behind you. When you reach the forge, {npc} is standing in the doorway with folded arms, and behind {him} the fire that does not go out is burning blue-white and so hot nobody can come within ten paces. The lord's men go home. There are no spear-heads.

fail.log: You go in by night and are caught at the inner gate and badly beaten. But in the confusion the grandchild slips out, and runs all the way home, and when the lord's men come to the forge for their spears the fire that does not go out has gone out, cold as a stone, for the first time in a hundred years, and will not light for them. (-12 health)

choices.text: Tell {npc} to let the fire decide

effects.log: "Let it decide," you say. {npc} puts the first spear-head in the fire. It comes out brittle as a dry biscuit and breaks on the anvil. So does the second. So do all five hundred. The lord's officer, after a week, returns the grandchild in disgust and takes the spear-heads anyway, and the lord's war ends at the first shield wall, when every spear breaks.

events.text: Your sword, the one with the red line along its edge, is humming on its rack. It has hummed every evening this week, very faintly, a note like a kettle. Then word comes from the south: {npc} the smith is dead, and the fire that does not go out has gone out, and nobody in the family can light it.
events.arc: The Forge That Does Not Go Out

choices.text: Ride south and lay the sword in the cold forge

effects.log: You ride south and lay the sword across the cold coals in the dead forge, without knowing why. The red line along its edge glows, and the coals under it begin to smoke, and catch. The family weeps. When you lift the sword, the red line is gone from it, and the blade is just a blade, and in the forge the fire that does not go out is burning again.

choices.text: Ride south and help the family mourn

effects.log: You ride south and stand with the family at the grave. At dusk, a red bird lands on the cold anvil in the empty forge, and sits there a long time, with its feathers dull. Then it hops into the firebox and lies down in the cold ash, and the forge glows, and the fire that does not go out is lit again. The youngest grandchild is the smith now. You have your sword tempered there every ten years.

events.text: You have been hired to escort {npc}, a junior official of the court, carrying summer's new fire from the palace to the southern provinces in a covered bronze pot: apricot and jujube fire, rubbed in the palace, for the governors' offices. If it goes out on the road, the official will be disgraced. On the third day, in a downpour on a mountain pass, {npc} lifts the lid. The pot is cold.

choices.text: Make new fire on the spot, of the right wood

ok.log: You find apricot wood in a farmer's orchard below the pass, and jujube from a hedge, and saw and saw in the shelter of a rock until your hands are raw and a spark comes. Summer's fire, rubbed from summer's wood: the rite is kept, if not the palace's flame. {npc} weeps with relief. And when you blow the spark into the pot, a small red shape flickers in it for a moment, as if somebody had come to check.

fail.log: You saw at the wet wood until your hands bleed and get nothing. {npc} sits in the mud with the cold pot in {his} lap. Then, out of the rain, a red bird the size of a crow lands on the rim of the pot, looks at both of you with something like pity, and steps inside, and the pot is warm. Neither of you ever reports it. (-3 health)

choices.text: Tell {npc} to report the truth: the fire went out in the rain

effects.log: "Report it," you say. "The rain is not your crime." {npc} is quiet a long while, and then nods. When you lift the lid to show the governor's clerk the cold pot, it is not cold. It is burning, small and clear and red. {npc} goes white. The governor's clerk takes it without a word. That night {npc} writes an honest report anyway, and is not believed, and is promoted.

events.text: {npc}, the official who carried summer's fire, is a provincial governor now, and has sent for you. A great house in the province has refused to change its fire for sixty years. Fevers in every room. A barn burned. Servants quarrelling with knives. The head of the house says the old fire is a family treasure and the governor may come and put it out personally.

choices.text: Go with {npc} and talk to the head of the house

effects.log: You sit with the head of the house a whole afternoon, drinking barley tea, and talk about grandmothers. At last, near dusk, the head of the house admits the fire frightens the whole household now; it roars at night. The old fire is put out with rites, and new fire brought, summer's wood, and that night something in the dead ashes crackles, quietly, like a long sigh. The fevers go down within the month.

choices.text: Go into the kitchen and look at the fire

ok.log: You go in alone. The fire in the old hearth is white at the heart and too loud and the air round it shimmers. It reaches for your sleeve. You do not let it. You hold it down with your own qi, like holding an animal still for the bonesetter, until {npc}'s men can carry the new fire in and lay it. The old fire goes out with a cry like a hawk. The house sleeps that night, all of it.

fail.log: You go in alone and the fire leaps at you and you come out with your sleeves alight. {npc} has the house cleared and the hearth flooded by order. The old fire goes out screaming. You are bandaged for a month, and the house is well by the end of it. (-10 health)

events.text: At the ferry landing below the mountain temple, {npc}, an old monk, keeps a lantern lit all night for travellers on the river. The lantern has not gone out in forty years, in any wind, and its light is red, not yellow. You have stopped for the night at the temple, and {npc} sits with you on the landing and asks, out of nowhere: "What is fire? I have kept this one forty years and I still do not know."

choices.text: Answer: fire is what is given away

effects.log: "Fire is what is given away," you say, not knowing where it came from. "Kept, it burns. Given, it warms." {npc} looks at you a long time and then at the lantern. Inside it, the flame bows, very slightly. "Forty years," {npc} says. "And a traveller says it in one breath." {npc} laughs until {his} eyes are wet.

choices.text: Answer: I do not know either

effects.log: "I do not know either," you say. {npc} nods, satisfied, as if that were the right answer. You sit together in silence until a lost child comes walking along the dark bank toward the red light, crying, and {npc} gets up and takes the child's hand. "That," {npc} says over {his} shoulder, "is the nearest I have come."

choices.text: Ask {npc} what is inside the lantern

effects.log: "Look," {npc} says, and lifts the paper shade. Inside, on the wick, sitting in the flame as if it were a perch, is a tiny red bird no bigger than a thumb, asleep. {npc} lowers the shade gently. "It came the winter I first took the ferry lantern," {npc} says. "It has never said a word to me. I hope it likes the river."

events.text: Word comes from the ferry temple: {npc}, the old monk of the lantern, has died in meditation on the landing, with the lantern in {his} hands. The lantern has gone out for the first time in forty years. The temple has asked if you will come, because {npc} left your name.

choices.text: Go, and keep the lantern one night yourself

effects.npcPass: old age, in meditation on the ferry landing
effects.log: You go, and sit on the landing at dusk with the cold lantern on your knees. At full dark a small red light comes upriver, low over the water, and goes into the lantern, and the lantern is lit, red and steady. A lost traveller comes along the bank before midnight and finds the ferry. In the morning a young monk takes the lantern from you, and you show them how to sit with it. You do not tell them what is inside.

choices.text: Go, and carry the cold lantern to the cremation

effects.npcPass: old age, in meditation on the ferry landing
effects.log: You carry the cold lantern behind the bier to the pyre. When the pyre is lit, the lantern in your hands catches too, from the inside, without anyone touching it, and burns red and steady while {npc} burns. Afterwards it is still lit. The temple hangs it at the ferry landing again. It has not gone out since, you hear.

events.text: {npc} keeps the ferry at the wide river crossing where you go to fish, a weathered, kind, solitary person who talks to the ferry lantern every night as if it were a friend. This summer {npc} is different: singing on the pole, laughing at nothing. There is a stranger who crosses every evening at dusk and back at dawn, in a red robe, never paying, never speaking to anyone else. {npc} has asked you, shyly, what you think of the stranger.

choices.text: Say you are happy for {npc}

effects.log: "I am happy for you," you say. {npc} goes pink to the ears and nearly drops the pole in the river. That evening the stranger in red nods to you from the bow, gravely, as to someone who has been introduced. Up close, the stranger's eyes are a colour you have only ever seen in a forge.

choices.text: Warn {npc}: there is something not human about the stranger

effects.log: "There is something not quite human about them," you say. {npc} laughs. "I know," {npc} says. "The lantern goes out when they get in the boat. Every time. And comes back on when they get out." A pause. "I do not mind. Do you think I should?" You do not know what to say.

choices.text: Watch the stranger cross, one evening, from the reeds

effects.log: You watch from the reeds. The stranger in red steps into the ferry and the lantern goes out at once. They cross talking, low, the two of them, about nothing at all: fish, the weather, the price of rope. On the far bank the stranger steps out, and the lantern lights again, and a red bird goes up from the willows into the dusk. You go home and tell no one.

events.text: The summer is over. The stranger in red has stopped coming to the ferry. {npc} still talks to the lantern every night, and keeps the ferry, and is very quiet. You find {npc} one evening on the landing, holding a single red feather, warm, that was left on the bow seat.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and say nothing

effects.log: You sit on the landing with {npc} until the stars are out. The lantern burns red and steady. At last {npc} says: "It said it could not stay. It said it gets older slower than the river. It said it would come by." You stay till the last ferry. Every summer after that, on one evening, the lantern goes out for the length of one crossing.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the stranger will be back

effects.log: "It will come back," you say, with no idea whether it is true. {npc} looks at you, and nods, and puts the feather inside {his} jacket. The next summer, on the longest day, the lantern goes out for the length of one crossing, and {npc} comes back across the river singing.

events.text: {npc} the ferry-keeper is very old, and has not poled the ferry in years. You visit on the longest day. At dusk, a stranger in a red robe comes down the far bank, exactly as young as forty summers ago, and stands there looking across the water.

choices.text: Pole the ferry over for {npc}

effects.log: You pole the ferry over. The lantern goes out the moment the stranger steps aboard. You pole back in the dark, and neither of you speaks, and {npc} is waiting on the landing, leaning on a stick. The stranger gets out and takes {npc}'s hands. You go up to the house and leave them there. In the morning {npc} has died, smiling, on the landing, and the lantern is lit, and nobody is on the far bank.

choices.text: Help {npc} down to the landing and leave them the ferry

effects.log: You help {npc} down to the landing and into the ferry, and push it off, and the lantern goes out. In the dusk you watch the old ferry-keeper pole across, slow and sure, the way {npc} did for years. On the far bank a red robe stands waiting. The ferry does not come back that night. In the morning it is tied up neatly at the far bank, empty, and the lantern on it is burning red.

events.text: Buddha's birthday in a southern county town, and you have been asked to help with the falling-fire festival: oak charcoal ground fine and rolled in paper round a cotton wick, hundreds of them, hung on ropes over the pond. At dark they are lit one by one from rafts, and the burning charcoal falls like petals onto the water. Halfway through, one whole rope of them flares up all at once, far too bright, and the fire on it begins to dance.

choices.text: Pole your raft closer to see

effects.log: You pole closer. Along the rope a red bird is hopping from wick to wick, lighting each one with a touch of its beak, faster than any raft-crew, and the fire falling behind it falls slower and brighter and redder than charcoal can. The crowd on the bank is shouting with joy. Nobody but you can see the bird. When it reaches the end of the rope it looks back at you, pleased with itself, and is gone.

choices.text: Shout to cut the rope before it spreads

effects.log: "Cut it!" you shout, and the raft-crew cuts the rope, and the whole burning line drops into the pond with a hiss. The crowd groans. On the bank, something red sits on a willow branch with its feathers puffed out, sulking magnificently, until the last wick is lit. Then it flies down and lights the last one again, and the crowd cheers, and you decide not to argue.

events.text: The falling-fire festival again, years later, and this time the county is in mourning: a flood took half the lower town in the spring. The magistrate wants to cancel the festival. The old people want it held, for the dead, as it always was. They have asked you, because of the year the fire danced, to decide.

choices.text: Hold it, for the dead

effects.log: It is held. The charcoal falls on the pond like petals, slow and red, and the whole town stands on the bank without a sound. At the end, one last light comes down from the dark, not on a rope, falling slowly from very high, and goes out on the water exactly in the middle of the pond. The old people bow to the place. So do you.

choices.text: Hold it small: one rope, one raft

effects.log: One rope, one raft, lit by you alone. The petals of fire fall onto the black water in silence. Then the rope beside it, the one nobody hung, begins to burn too, and the next, all the way round the pond, ropes of falling light hanging from nothing. You stand on the raft until the last petal goes out. Nobody in the county ever explains it, and nobody tries.

events.text: {npc}, an alchemist from the capital with red-stained fingers and a great deal of money, has hired you for a hunt. The quarry is a bird. Red, {npc} says, the size of a crane, nesting on a cliff of the southern sea. One feather of it is worth a mine of cinnabar; a whole bird would make ink for every talisman in the kingdom. The net {npc} unrolls on the cliff top is a silk so fine it shimmers, and it does not burn. At dawn, far out over the sea, a red light is coming in.

choices.text: Hold your end of the net

ok.log: The bird comes in low and the net goes up and for one moment it is in it, a whole burning crane-sized bird tangled in shimmering silk, screaming like a kettle. Then it does something with its fire you do not understand, and the net is empty and smouldering at one corner and the bird is gone over the sea, minus three tail feathers that lie on the rock. {npc} gathers them up with shaking hands and pays you twenty-five taels. You do not sleep well for a month.

fail.log: The bird comes in and sees the net and does not even slow down: it goes straight through the middle of it, and the net, which does not burn, melts instead, and you are holding a handful of hot silk that sticks to your palm. The bird circles once, very high, looking down at you, and goes. {npc} curses for an hour. You are not paid. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let go of the net and shout a warning

effects.log: You drop your end and shout, as loud as you can, out over the sea. The red light veers away from the cliff, high, and passes over the two of you like a second sunrise, and you feel the heat of it on your face. {npc} looks at you with a cold, careful hatred. "I will remember that," {npc} says. You believe it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what happens to the bird after

effects.log: "After?" {npc} looks puzzled. "It is ground. Feather, bone, all of it. In a mortar, with mercury, for nine days." You put your end of the net down on the rock. {npc} sees your face, and sighs, and rolls up the net. "There is always another hired hand," {npc} says. "And it is always the same bird."

events.text: {npc}, the cinnabar alchemist, has sent you a gift: a talisman written in a red so bright it hurts your eyes, against every ghost and fever. With it, a letter. {npc} has the bird's nest now, {npc} says: found it on the cliff, in the ash of an old beacon. The bird comes back to it every spring. This spring, the net will be ready, and {npc} would like you to be there, as an old hunting friend.

choices.text: Go to the cliff before {npc} does, and spoil the net

ok.log: You get there a night early and find {npc}'s people setting the net. You cut it, all of it, and fight {npc} on the cliff edge in the dark, briefly, and leave {npc} sitting in the shreds of the silk. At dawn the red bird comes in from the sea and lands on its nest in the old beacon, and sits there looking at the two of you, and at the ruined net, and at you. Then it settles down and sleeps.

fail.log: You get there a night early and {npc} is waiting for you. It goes badly. You end up at the bottom of the cliff path with a broken arm. But the noise carried. At dawn the red bird does not come to its nest. It never comes to that cliff again. {npc} sits by the empty nest all spring. (-12 health)

choices.text: Burn the talisman, and write back: no

effects.log: You burn the talisman in your brazier. It burns red, hot and long, much longer than paper should, as if the ink in it were glad to be fire again. You write back one word. {npc} does not write again. In the spring you hear that a net was set on a southern cliff and that it caught nothing, because a beacon soldier on the next hill lit two fires at dawn for no reason, and the bird turned away.

events.text: A hungry ghost has been taking the breath of children in a mountain village, and the village has sent for you, and for a shaman. The shaman has brought talismans written in ordinary red, and they are not working: the ghost laughs at them. The shaman says, low, that there is one red that always works, the red of the bird of the south, and that you can buy it in the capital, for a price, from people who net birds.

choices.text: Fight the ghost with your own art

ok.log: You meet it at the village gate at midnight with nothing but your own qi and a torch, and it is a long night, and a cold one. But at dawn it is gone, scattered like mist, and the children wake pink-cheeked. You did not need the bird's red. You are glad you did not.

fail.log: It is too strong for you. At the worst of it, with the cold of the ghost in your chest, a red light comes down out of the night over the village, and the ghost shrieks and goes. Not ink. The bird itself, passing. It does not stop. You lie in the snow at the gate and laugh, weakly, at the thought of buying it in a shop. (-12 health)

choices.text: Smear the gate with red-bean porridge and keep watch

effects.log: You cook a vat of red-bean porridge and fling it on every gate, as the grandmothers do on the longest night, and keep watch. The ghost comes and goes round the village twice and cannot find a gate it likes. Toward dawn it gives up. It is not the bird's red. It is the people's red, and it is enough, this once.

events.text: In the capital, at a great house, you see it: a whole wall of talismans written in the red of the bird of the south, glowing faintly in the dark corridor. Ink for a thousand charms. The house is the safest in the city from every ghost and fever. The master of the house shows them off proudly. "A whole bird," the master says. "My grandfather bought it."

choices.text: Say quietly what that ink was

effects.log: You say it, quietly, to the master of the house: that the ink was a living thing, once, that came down to cold kitchens. The master laughs, and then stops laughing, and looks at the wall for a long time. A month later you hear the house has given the talismans away, one by one, to every poor village with a ghost in it. It is the best thing that could be done with them.

choices.text: Touch one, and listen

effects.log: You touch one with a fingertip. It is warm. For a moment you hear, very far away, a sound like a kettle, or a bird, or a summer afternoon. Then nothing. You leave the house and walk a long time. On the way home a red bird crosses the sky high over the city, going south, very fast, and you are glad, absurdly glad, that there is still one.

events.text: An invading fleet is coming up the narrow strait on the night tide, three times your ships, and you command the southern squadron. Your captains have filled twelve old fishing boats with pine brush and sulphur to send down on the tide as fire-ships. The wind is wrong: it will blow them back on your own line. At midnight, as you are about to give the order to scuttle them, the wind dies completely, and the sky above the strait goes red, like dawn in the wrong place.

choices.text: Send the fire-ships now, on the tide alone

ok.log: You send them. With no wind, the tide carries them straight down the strait into the enemy's packed line, and they catch, all twelve, at once, as if lit from above. The strait is fire from shore to shore. By dawn the invading fleet is broken and running. Your captains swear a red shape as big as a hill flew low over the fire-ships all night. You put it in no report.

fail.log: You send them, and half of them ground on a sandbar and burn uselessly, and the enemy comes through the gap, and it is a long bloody night, galley against galley. But at the worst of it the grounded fire-ships flare up white and the enemy line, lit up like noon, loses its nerve and turns. You hold the strait. Barely. (-14 health)

choices.text: Look up, and wait for a sign

effects.log: You wait, looking up at the red sky, while your captains fret. Then something in the red moves, an enormous wing-shape, and banks, and points, unmistakably, at the far side of the strait, where a second enemy squadron you never saw is hiding behind the headland. You send the fire-ships there instead. It is the battle of your life, and you win it, and you never tell anyone who pointed.

choices.text: Scuttle the fire-ships: you will not burn men alive

effects.log: You scuttle them. Your captains think you have lost your mind. You fight the invaders galley to galley at dawn, hard and costly, and turn them back with fewer deaths on both sides than fire would have made. Above the strait, as the sun comes up, the red in the sky fades slowly, and you have the strange feeling that you were watched, and not judged badly.

events.text: After the battle in the strait, the coast villages have started flying red banners on their boats. Your captains fly them too. The court has noticed: a minister has written that a red bird on banners is a southern superstition that smells of rebellion, and the banners must come down.

choices.text: Write to the court: the banners stay

ok.log: You write a letter so careful and so plain that the minister, reading it in open court, cannot find a word to object to: the banners are the colour of the south, as the classics say; in front, the vermilion bird. The king laughs and lets the banners fly. They fly for generations. Every coast child grows up knowing the red banner means the fleet is coming home.

fail.log: Your letter offends the minister and the banners are ordered down. They come down. But the fishermen paint the red bird on the inside of their hulls instead, where no minister will ever look, and on every boat on the southern coast there is a red bird under the waterline, looking down into the dark.

choices.text: Take the banners down, and keep one

effects.log: You take them down, to keep the peace. You keep one, folded, in your sea-chest. Years later, when you are old and the fleet is someone else's, you fly it once more from your own little boat on the summer solstice, and a red shape comes down out of the noon and circles your mast three times. The coast villages talk about it for a generation.

events.text: {npc}, the chief geomancer of the court, has asked for you. The sharp peak south of the capital, the fire mountain the palace has always guarded against with a pond and a gate-name hung on end and stone fire-eaters at its door, has been glowing at night. Something lives on it now. Three fires in the city this spring. {npc} wants it off the mountain, and has heard that you can climb where others cannot.

choices.text: Climb the fire mountain and talk to whatever is there

effects.log: You climb all night. At the top, in a hollow of the bare rock that is warm as a stove, a great red bird is sitting with its back to the capital, looking south. It does not move when you come. "They dug a pond at me," it says, without turning round. "They hung their gate-name sideways at me. I came to see what they were so afraid of." It considers. "Their fires were their own. I only watched." You climb down at dawn with that to tell.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether the fires were really from the mountain

effects.log: {npc} is offended, and then, being honest, looks up the fire office's records with you. The three fires: a drunk lamp-seller, a careless dyer, a kitchen nobody had swept in years. Nothing from the mountain. {npc} rolls up the records and looks south a long time. "Then the glow," {npc} says, "is just something keeping watch. Like us."

choices.text: Help {npc} deepen the pond at the south gate

effects.log: You help with the digging, which is not what you were hired for, but {npc} is very old and the labourers are slow. The pond is made deeper and wider. That night the glow on the mountain is brighter than ever, and has a distinct air of someone laughing. {npc} sighs. "Well," {npc} says, "at least the carp are happy."

events.text: A great fire in the capital: a spring noon, a hard northwest wind, a fire from a servant's quarters south of the market, and it is running across the roofs faster than a horse. Two thousand houses are in its path. {npc} the geomancer, white-faced, says it is the fire mountain's doing at last. Up on the peak to the south, the red glow is very bright.

choices.text: Climb a roof and fight the fire at its head

ok.log: You get ahead of it, roof to roof, tearing thatch off with your hands to make a gap. And over the fire's head, coming down from the south against the wind, a red shape as big as a palace hall goes back and forth along the line of flame, and wherever it passes the fire falls back, as if called home. By evening it is out. Hundreds of houses are lost, not thousands. {npc}, black with soot, says nothing about the mountain ever again.

fail.log: You get ahead of it and the smoke drops you on a burning roof. Somebody drags you down. When you wake, the fire is out, and the city is saying a red bird came down from the southern mountain against the wind and called the fire back like a dog. {npc} sits by your bed. "I was wrong," {npc} says. "It came to help." (-16 health)

choices.text: Organise the bucket lines and the fire-breaks

effects.log: You take charge of a street, then a ward: bucket lines from the wells, houses pulled down for fire-breaks, the old and the small sent north. It is the hardest day of your life. At the end of it the fire stops at your last fire-break, and turns, and lies down. Above the break, a red bird is sitting on a ridge-pole, watching, black with soot. You bow to it. It bows back.

events.text: After the great fire the court has founded a fire office, with watchmen, bells, and a ledger. {npc} the old geomancer has been made its first head, and has opened a file in the ledger on the fire mountain and what lives there. {npc} wants your help writing the first entry, because you are the only one who has spoken to it.

choices.text: Write that it is a guardian

effects.log: You write it plainly: a guardian of the south, which keeps watch over the capital and does not start its fires. {npc} reads it twice and signs below. The file is kept for five hundred years. Every head of the fire office reads it on their first day. Not one of them ever orders the pond filled in, either. "Both," one of them writes in the margin, centuries later. "It is both."

choices.text: Write that it is dangerous, and should be watched

effects.log: You write it honestly: a power of fire that sits facing the capital, that helped once and could do otherwise. Watch it, respect it, keep the pond. {npc} signs below. That night the glow on the mountain is very bright, and you have the uncomfortable feeling it was reading over your shoulder, and did not disagree.

events.text: An officer of heaven's fire office has come down out of the clouds onto your mountain with a ledger and a long bronze snuffer. Heaven has an account to settle, the officer says: seven fires in the south, given by a bird to humans, unlicensed. A hearth, a kiln, a beacon, a ferry lantern, a field fire, a rite candle, a magistrate's lamp. They are to be put out tonight. The officer wants a guide, and you know the south.

choices.text: Refuse to guide, and stand in the way

roll.foeName: The officer of the fire office

ok.log: You refuse, and the officer tries to go past, and you stop it. It is a strange fight, against a snuffer that eats your qi like a candle-flame. At the end of it the officer is sitting on your mountain rubbing a bruised wrist and looking at you with reluctant respect. "Heaven will hear of this," it says. "Good," you say. "Tell heaven a human stood up for seven fires."

fail.log: You refuse and the officer puts you down with the snuffer, coldly, efficiently, and steps over you. But it took long enough. By the time the officer reaches the first fire, a hearth in a village kitchen, a red bird is already sitting in it, wings spread over it, and the officer, after a long look, writes something in the ledger and goes back up to heaven with nothing put out. (-16 health)

choices.text: Guide it, and argue the case for each fire as you go

effects.log: You guide it, and at every fire you argue: the hearth that kept a widow alive, the beacon that saved a coast, the lantern that brought a lost child home, the lamp by which a magistrate read an honest case. At the seventh fire the officer closes the ledger. "Licensed," it says, wearily, "all seven, on the testimony of a human of the south." It goes back up. The fires burn on.

choices.text: Go ahead of it, and warn the keepers

effects.log: You run ahead of it all night, from fire to fire, waking the keepers: the old woman with the fire jar, the potter, the beacon captain, the ferry-keeper. Each of them sits up with their fire till dawn, guarding it with their own hands. When the officer comes, at each one there is a human sitting by the fire, and it will not put out a fire a human is guarding. By dawn it gives up.

events.text: The officer of the fire office has come back, alone, without its snuffer. It sits down on a rock on your mountain and asks, almost shyly, whether you would show it one of the seven fires. Just one. It has put out a great many fires in its time, it says, and has never once sat by one.

choices.text: Take it to a village hearth at supper

effects.log: You take it, in a plain grey robe, to a village kitchen at supper time, where a family is eating by a hearth that has burned for nine generations. The family feeds you both without asking who you are. The officer eats in silence, looking at the fire. When you leave, it says: "I did not know they laughed by them." It does not come back again. But the fire office, you hear, puts out a great many fewer hearths after that.

choices.text: Take it to the beacon hill at dusk

effects.log: You take it to the beacon hill on the southern coast at dusk, and the captain lights the one fire, all is well. The officer watches the answering fire light on the next hill, and the next, and the next, a chain of single fires up the dark coast. "Each one says: we are safe," you tell it. The officer stays until midnight. It leaves its ledger on the beacon hut's step. Nobody comes back for it.

events.text: {npc}, a grandmaster of the north who has never lost a duel, has announced to every sect in the land that at noon on the summer solstice, on the southern summit, {npc} will challenge the bird of summer itself. You are asked, as a neutral master, to witness. At noon the sky to the south goes red, and {npc} draws.

choices.text: Witness, as asked, and keep out of it

effects.log: You witness. It is not a duel. {npc} stands in the heat for an hour with the sword up, and the red in the sky does nothing at all but get hotter. At last {npc}'s sword droops, and {npc} sits down on the scorched rock, and the red light comes down, a little, as if to look. "It would not even fight me," {npc} says to you afterwards. "I have never been so beaten."

choices.text: Step in and tell {npc} it is a summer, not a sect

effects.log: You step into the heat beside {npc} and say, "It is the summer. You cannot beat a summer. You can only wait for autumn." {npc} stares at you, and then at the sky, and then laughs, a short, real laugh, and sheathes the sword. The red light above the summit flickers, as if it were laughing too. You both go down to a teahouse in the valley and raise your cups to autumn.

choices.text: Draw your own sword and stand beside {npc}

roll.foeName: The heat of the southern summit

ok.log: You stand beside {npc}, swords up, in the heat, for one whole hour. Neither of you falls. At the end of it the red light comes down close, enormous, a great bird made of noon, and bows to the two of you, as one bows to guests who have stayed late out of politeness. Then it goes. You and {npc} are famous for a century, for a duel in which nothing happened.

fail.log: You stand beside {npc} in the heat and the heat takes you, and you wake in the shade of a rock with {npc} pouring water over your head. "It did not touch us," {npc} says. "It did not need to. Summer is summer." You agree, with your head pounding, that summer is summer. (-14 health)

events.text: {npc}, the grandmaster who challenged the summer, has taken a new student, and has asked you to come to the first lesson. It is at noon, at midsummer, on a bare hill. There are no swords. {npc} sits the student down in the full sun and says: "Today we learn to wait for autumn."

choices.text: Sit and wait with them

effects.log: You sit with them all afternoon in the burning sun. Nobody speaks. Near dusk, a cool wind comes down from the west, the first of autumn, and the student begins to cry without knowing why, and {npc} nods, very satisfied. On the way down, a red bird passes far overhead, going south, and dips its wings. {npc} bows to it, a full formal bow, the first you have ever seen {npc} give anyone.

choices.text: Tease {npc} about the lesson

effects.log: "You lost a duel to the weather," you say, "and now you teach it." {npc} laughs. "I lost a duel to the weather," {npc} agrees, "and it was the best teacher I ever had." The student, sweating in the sun, looks at both of you as if you were mad, which, by noon, you both somewhat are.

events.text: A messenger has come for you, a young swallow that lands on your windowsill and will not leave until you follow it. It leads you south for nine days to a high peak above the sea. The bird of the south is there, enormous now, every feather a flame, and it says: "I go up to my seat at noon. Heaven wants a witness from below. Someone who can say what I did here."

choices.text: Agree, and ask it to tell you everything it did

effects.log: It tells you. The fires, all of them: the hearth and the kiln and the beacon and the lantern, the field that ran wild once, the keeper who turned, the village the swallows left. The warm verses and the ugly ones. It does not skip any. At noon it rises, and you stand on the peak and tell heaven what you heard, all of it, out loud, and your voice does not shake. When you come down you are a different person.

choices.text: Agree, and tell it you already know: you have seen its fires

effects.log: "I have seen your fires," you say. "I have sat by them." The great bird looks at you a long time. "Then that is the record," it says, "and better than mine." At noon it rises toward the red stars, and you stand on the peak and say what you have seen, a widow's kitchen, a ferry lantern, a beacon on a coast, plainly, like a farmer listing a harvest. It is enough.

choices.text: Ask why heaven wants a human

effects.log: "Because the fires were for you," the bird says, puzzled that you need to ask. "Who else could say whether they warmed?" At noon it rises. You stand on the peak in the blazing light and say that they warmed. Somewhere far above, a voice like a great book closing says: noted.

events.text: Every summer since you witnessed the bird take its seat, the solstice comes to you as a guest comes: on time, warm, with a small gift. This year the gift is a swallow on your windowsill with a single red feather in its beak, and behind it a whole flock, waiting, as if they have been told to escort you somewhere.

choices.text: Follow them

effects.log: You follow them south to the sea. On the beach, on the longest day, at noon, the sky goes red, and for one moment something enormous looks down at you out of the sun, and dips its wings, the way a friend waves from a boat. Then the swallows wheel away home and you walk back north, nine days, happier than you have been in years.

choices.text: Thank them and stay home

effects.log: You thank them and stay home. The swallows sit on your eaves all day, and at noon, when the sun is highest, they all sing at once, and the whole village comes out to listen. The red feather you put on your family shrine. It is warm every summer.

events.text: You have reached a height where very few humans stand. On a warm rock above the southern sea, one summer evening, a red bird the size of a temple lands beside you, folds its wings, and says, a little stiffly, as if it had practised: "You are a human at my level. I have never had a friend who was not a keeper of one of my fires. Would you be one?"
events.arc: A Friend at the Same Height

choices.text: Say yes, and pour it tea

effects.log: You say yes, and pour it tea, in your second cup. It drinks it in one gulp, boiling, and says it is very good. You talk until moonrise: about nothing, about the weather, about the swallows' gossip and the price of a sect's goodwill. It laughs at your jokes like a kettle. You realise, walking home, that it has never had anyone to talk to about nothing.

choices.text: Ask what a friend of the south is expected to do

effects.log: "Nothing," it says. "That is the point. Everyone wants something from me: fire, a sign, a feather, a war won. I want someone who wants nothing." You think about it. "I want one thing," you say. "I want you to visit." It is quiet for a moment. Then it says yes, with what sounds suspiciously like a lump in its throat.

choices.text: Tease it: friends do not ask so formally

effects.log: "Friends do not ask like that," you say. "They just come back next week." It ruffles every feather at once, mortified, and the rock under it smokes. Then it laughs, so hard a pine down the slope catches, and you have to put it out together. It comes back the next week. And the next.

events.text: Your friend, the bird of the south, has come to your door in a terrible temper: an envoy of heaven said something about its record at a council, and it swallowed the insult, and it has been swallowing it for a month. The edge of your veranda is already smoking.
events.arc: A Friend at the Same Height

choices.text: Make it sing it out

effects.log: "Sing it," you say. "All of it. I will not mind." It sings. It is a terrible song, furious and funny, with the envoy's name in every verse. The whole valley hears it. By the end it is laughing, and the smoke has stopped, and the envoy's name has become, in your valley, a word for someone who talks too much. It goes home cool and light.

choices.text: Let it shout, and put out what catches

effects.log: You let it shout. Three trees and your woodpile catch. You put them out, one after another, while it rages. When it is done it looks at the black woodpile and goes very quiet and ashamed. "Better your woodpile than heaven's archive," you say. It brings you a new woodpile the next day, of apricot and jujube, and you burn it all winter and are never cold.

events.text: Your first errand in the Upper Realm: carry one live coal from the first of the seven southern halls to the last, on foot, without letting it go out. It is a test every new immortal of the south is given, the hall steward says, and most fail it. The coal is the size of a plum. It is very hot. The halls are very long, and in each one something tries to make you put it down.

choices.text: Walk slowly, and talk to it

effects.log: You walk slowly and talk to the coal, all the way, as you might talk to a frightened child: about the hall, about the clouds, about the kitchen fire of your childhood. In the third hall a wind tries to blow it out and it burns brighter. In the fifth a voice offers you a cool cup of water and you walk on. At the seventh door, the coal is brighter than when you started. The steward looks at it, and at you. "It liked you," the steward says.

choices.text: Walk fast and shield it with your own qi

ok.log: You walk fast and wrap it in your own qi like a hand around a candle. In the fourth hall something tries to snatch it and you do not let go. Your palms blister. At the seventh door the coal is still alight, and so, just, are you. The steward nods, once. "Few carry it fast," the steward says. "Fewer carry it well."

fail.log: You walk fast and in the sixth hall the coal goes grey in your hands. You stand there, desperate. Then you breathe on it, very gently, the way you would breathe on a spark in a cold jar, and it glows again. You walk the last hall slowly. The steward says nothing about the sixth hall. The steward does not need to. (-10 health)

events.text: The steward of the southern halls tells you where the coal you carried went: into the hearth of a very old house below, in a cold country of the far north, where the fire had gone out for the first time in six hundred years. The family woke to find it lit. The steward thinks you should see it.

choices.text: Go down and look in at the window

effects.log: You go down, invisible, and look in at the window. A family round a hearth, three generations, in a house where the snow comes up to the eaves. The grandmother is laying a pine needle on the coals. You stand in the snow outside for a long time. When you go back up, the steward does not ask how it was.

choices.text: Ask why the south sends fire to the north

effects.log: "Because fire that is kept, burns," says the steward, as if quoting, "and fire that is given, warms." A pause. "The bird says it to every new immortal. I think it is the only law the south has." You think about it all the way through the seven halls, back to your own.

events.text: The council of the Four Guardians has asked for your testimony. The question before it is the fires of the south: whether the bird of the south has kept them as a guardian should, or burned more than it warmed. You were a human of the south once. You have seen its fires. The council's terrace is very quiet. The red glow at its southern edge is quieter than the rest.

choices.text: Testify to the warm fires and the burned ones alike

effects.log: You tell them all of it: the hearths and the beacon and the lantern, and the field fire that ran up a mountain once, and the county where the swallows did not come back for a generation. You skip nothing. When you are done, the red glow at the southern edge brightens, very slightly, and you understand that you said what it would have said, and that it is grateful you did not make it prettier.

choices.text: Speak only of the warm fires: the burned ones are its own to tell

effects.log: You speak of the hearths and the lanterns and the beacon on the coast, and stop. "The rest is its to tell," you say. The council is silent. Then the red glow at the southern edge says, in a voice like a summer afternoon: "I will tell it." And does, every ugly verse, while you stand there. You think it wanted someone to start with the warm part.

choices.text: Ask the council what it would have done in the bird's place

effects.log: "What would you have done," you ask, "with seven fires and a quick temper and the whole south cold?" The black glow at the northern edge rumbles, amused. The blue glow at the eastern edge goes quiet. The white glow at the western edge says, "Badly." The council laughs, all four quarters of it, and the question is closed in the south's favour.

events.text: After your testimony, the bird of the south has sent you an invitation: to sit in the gallery, once, at the council of the Four. You go. When the newest guardian of some far direction comes in, young and nervous, it is the bird of the south that rises first, and bows first, lowest, before anyone else has moved.

choices.text: Ask it afterwards why it bows first

effects.log: "Because I was the youngest once," it says, "and had to bow to everyone, and it was awful. And then a human at a table raised a cup to an empty seat before they sat in their own, and I thought: that. That is courtesy. Going first." It looks at you sideways. "Some humans did that," it says. "Some sat in the seat. I liked them too."

choices.text: Bow to the newcomer too, from the gallery

effects.log: You stand up in the gallery and bow to the newcomer, as low as the bird did. The newcomer, who had been shaking, sees the bird and you bowing, and straightens, and bows back to both, and the council begins. Afterwards the bird says nothing about it. But your seat in the gallery is kept for you, from then on, with your name on it, in a looping hand.

events.text: A summons from the Red Emperor of summer: there is a small world beyond the edge of heaven that has never been warm. Its people have never seen a summer. The Emperor asks you to carry summer there. Not to stay, the summons says. Only to carry it, and give it, and come home.

choices.text: Go, and give it all at once

effects.log: You go, and on the frozen plain you open your hands, and summer goes out of them all at once: heat, light, green, the smell of wet earth. The ice cracks. The people come out of their stone houses and stand in the first warm air they have ever felt and do not know what to do with their faces. You come home before the first harvest. You never see what they grow. You do not need to.

choices.text: Go, and teach them to keep a fire first

effects.log: You go, and before you give them summer you sit with them for a season and teach them to keep a fire: a jar, ash to bank it at night, one pine needle in the morning, new wood each season. Only when every house has a fire do you open your hands and let the summer out. When you leave they give you, as a farewell, a little clay fire jar of their own making, banked with their own ash. It is the best gift you have ever had.

events.text: A message reaches you from the world you carried summer to. It is written on a clay tablet, warm to the touch. It says that the summers have gone on coming, every year, though no one carries them; and that this year, for the first time, the swallows came.

choices.text: Go and see the swallows

effects.log: You go. Under the eaves of every stone house there is a mud nest, and swallows going in and out, and the people of the cold world standing in the yards watching them with their mouths open. One swallow, older than the rest, lands on your shoulder, and you know whose messenger it is. You stay a whole summer this time.

choices.text: Send back a gourd seed

effects.log: You send back one gourd seed with the messenger, and a note: plant it by a kind house. A year later a second tablet comes: the gourd grew, and was full of rice, and the people of the cold world now argue every spring about which house is the kindest, so as to plant the seeds there. You think that is the best thing a world could argue about.

events.text: {npc}, a sovereign of the Upper Realm with a court of a thousand immortals, wants the south. Not to rule it: to own it. {npc}'s court would be the court summer comes from; {npc}'s name would be in every solstice rite. {npc} has asked you, as a sovereign of equal standing, to support the claim before heaven, and offers a great deal in return.

choices.text: Refuse: the south is not a thing to own

effects.log: "The south is not a thing," you say. "It is a direction, and a season, and a bird with a temper." {npc} is very cold with you for a century. But the claim is never brought, because you said it in front of {npc}'s court, and half of them were human once, and remembered summers.

choices.text: Suggest {npc} ask the bird

effects.log: "Ask the bird," you say. {npc} does, to your astonishment, in full state, with a herald. The bird listens to the whole proclamation, and then laughs so hard that the herald's scroll catches fire. {npc} withdraws the claim the same day. "I see," {npc} says to you afterwards, with dignity. "Summer has a sense of humour." "Summer has a temper," you say. "The humour is how it keeps it."

choices.text: Stand against the claim before heaven, formally

ok.log: You stand against it before heaven, and when {npc} tests you, as sovereigns do, you do not give ground. It is a long contest, all qi and no blood. In the end heaven rules: the south belongs to no court. {npc} bows to you, stiffly. The bird, you hear, sent you a peach.

fail.log: You stand against it and {npc} tests you and you give ground, and are hurt. But heaven rules against the claim anyway: the south belongs to no court. The bird, you hear, said at the council that the one who stood up and lost was worth more than the one who won. (-10 health)

events.text: {npc}, the sovereign who once claimed the south, has come to your hall in a plain robe, alone. {npc}'s court is cold this year, {npc} says. The hearths will not stay lit. Nobody will say why. {npc} wonders, stiffly, whether you might know someone who could help.

choices.text: Take {npc} to the southern halls to ask, politely

effects.log: You take {npc} through the seven southern halls, on foot, to the last. {npc} asks, politely, for fire, as a guest asks. The bird looks at {npc} a long time, and then gives a coal, small and red, and {npc} carries it home in both hands, slowly, all the way, and does not let it go out. {npc}'s court is warm that winter. {npc} sends the bird a peach every year after.

choices.text: Give {npc} a coal from your own hearth

effects.log: You give {npc} a coal from your own hearth, in a clay jar, banked with ash. "One pine needle in the morning," you say. {npc} looks at you as if you were mad, and takes it. A century later you visit {npc}'s court and find every hearth in it lit from your coal, and an old sovereign kneeling by the first of them with a bundle of pine needles.

events.text: You have been given a post in the archive of heaven, and on your first day the senior clerk shows you the shelf of the south. Every scroll on it is scorched at the edges. "The bird sings its record," the clerk explains, wearily. "We write it down. It laughs at the end, every time. We keep a bucket." Today the bird is coming to sing this year's record, and the clerk has a cold.

choices.text: Take down the song yourself, and keep the bucket close

effects.log: You take it down, every verse, warmth and ash, while the great bird sings in the archive door. It does not skip any. At the end it laughs, as promised, and the edge of your scroll catches, and you put it out with the bucket, calmly, and go on writing. The bird looks at you with new respect. "You did not flinch," it says. "The last clerk flinched."

choices.text: Ask it, politely, to laugh outside

effects.log: "Could you," you say, very politely, "laugh outside?" The whole archive goes silent. The bird stares at you. Then it walks out of the door, laughs, enormously, at the sky, so that a cloud catches, and comes back in, and finishes its song. For the first time in a thousand years the shelf of the south gets a scroll with clean edges. The senior clerk frames it.

events.text: A young envoy of heaven, very clever and very sure of it, has asked to read the shelf of the south. The envoy means to audit the bird at the next council, and has been making notes in a sharp, amused hand. You catch a glimpse of one: a joke about birds that sing their accounts.

choices.text: Warn the envoy about the bird's temper

effects.log: You take the envoy aside and tell them, quietly, about the bucket, and the scorched edges, and what happens when the bird swallows an insult too long. The envoy laughs, and then, reading the scorched edges, stops laughing. At the council the envoy asks every question, sharply, and makes not one joke. The bird, you hear, said afterwards that it was the best audit it ever had.

choices.text: Let the envoy learn for themselves

effects.log: You let them. At the council, you hear, the envoy made the joke. The bird swallowed it. Visibly. You spend the next month carrying cool water to the southern halls and suggesting songs. It is a long month. The envoy, to their credit, comes to apologise in person, and is given a peach, and a song with their name in every verse.

events.text: High on the mountain, the fire-field people are burning a slope for millet, as their grandparents did: cut the brush in spring, let it dry, burn it at noon on a still day, sow in the ash. You are passing on the ridge path when the wind changes. The fire turns and starts running uphill toward the pines, and toward you.

choices.text: Help them beat it back at the pine line

ok.log: You grab a wet mat and stand with the farmers at the pine line, beating at the sparks. The fire comes up the slope roaring, and then, at the very edge of the pines, as if it had hit a wall, it stops, and lies down, and goes back to burning the brush, slow and obedient. The farmers do not seem surprised. "It does that," the oldest says. "Our fire knows where the field ends."

fail.log: You stand at the pine line and the smoke takes you and you go down coughing. When you get up, the fire has stopped at the edge of the pines, exactly, and turned back into the brush. The farmers pour water on your face and tell you that the fire knows where the field ends. You do not argue. (-6 health)

choices.text: Run along the ridge and warn the next village

effects.log: You run along the ridge to warn the village in the next valley. By the time you get there and look back, the smoke on the slope has settled to a low grey haze over the burned field, and above it, very high, something red is turning in slow circles, like a hawk over its own ground.

events.text: The fire-field family on the mountain is in trouble. The eldest son, angry over a boundary, has set their field fire on a rival family's slope, and the rival's millet and a woodshed are gone. The rival wants blood. The fire-field grandmother has sent for you, because you were there the day the fire knew where the field ended.

choices.text: Make the son go to the rival and work off the debt

effects.log: You take the son down the mountain and stand beside him while he kneels to the rival family, and then you stay a month while he rebuilds their woodshed and sows their slope again. That autumn the two families harvest together. On the fire-field family's hearth, the grandmother tells you, the fire went cold for a week after the son did it, and only came back the day he knelt.

choices.text: Stand between the families until tempers cool

ok.log: The rival's eldest comes up the slope with a hoe and you take it off them, gently, and sit them down. It takes three days of sitting between the two families on the mountain path, and a great deal of rice wine, but nobody bleeds. The son pays in millet for three years. You think the fire would approve.

fail.log: The rival's eldest comes up with a hoe and you take the blow meant for the son. It ends it, oddly: the sight of a stranger's blood shames both families quiet. They settle in millet. The grandmother binds your arm herself and says the fire would have done worse. (-8 health)

events.text: You have been asked, as a respected guest, to attend the ancestral rite of a great lineage at midnight. The eldest of the lineage, {npc}, lights the rite candle on the shrine, a tall red candle that, the family says, has been lit from the same flame for three hundred years. Tonight, as the first bow begins, the candle gutters and nearly dies, and the tablets on the shrine rattle, all at once, as if something were knocking to get out.

choices.text: Shield the candle with your hands

effects.log: You cup your hands round the flame without thinking. It is a strange flame: it leans into your palms like an animal wanting warmth. It steadies. The tablets go still. {npc} finishes the rite without a tremor and afterwards takes you aside. "Someone in this house has been quarrelling over the inheritance," {npc} says. "The candle knows. The dead stay in their place only while the living keep theirs."

choices.text: Keep bowing, and let the family see to it

effects.log: You keep bowing. So does {npc}, slowly, with perfect calm. On the third bow the candle flares up red and tall, and the tablets go still, and a cold draught goes out of the shrine room through the door, like someone leaving. After the rite {npc} says only: "Somebody was not happy with this year's wine." You are almost sure it is a joke.

events.text: {npc}, the eldest of the lineage of the rite candle, has died, and the inheritance quarrel has broken out in the open. Two branches of the family have each taken half the shrine. The rite candle has gone out. And every night since, the family says, footsteps in the empty halls.

choices.text: Bring the two branches together before the dead candle

effects.npcPass: old age, the eldest of the line
effects.log: It takes a month of going from one branch to the other. At last they kneel together before the cold shrine, sulky and ashamed, and the youngest child of each branch lights a taper. When the two tapers touch the old candle together it catches, red and still, and the footsteps in the halls stop that night. You do not know who relit it, the children or something else. Both, you suspect.

choices.text: Sit up one night in the halls and speak to the footsteps

effects.npcPass: old age, the eldest of the line
effects.log: You sit up in the dark hall. At midnight the footsteps come, slow, old, a cane tapping. You say: "They are quarrelling. I am sorry." The footsteps stop beside you a long time. In the morning, the rite candle on the shrine is lit, though nobody lit it, and both branches of the family, frightened out of their wits, settle the inheritance by noon.

events.text: You are guarding {npc}, a county magistrate who has made enemies by being honest. {npc} works late every night by a single lamp, an old one with a red, very steady flame, and has noticed something strange about it: in its light, forged papers blacken at the edges, as if scorched, and honest ones do not. Tonight a rich landlord's deed to a whole village's paddies is on the desk, and it is going black.

choices.text: Advise {npc} to rule by what the lamp shows

effects.log: "Rule by it," you say. {npc} does, the next morning, in open court: the deed is forged, the paddies go back to the village. The landlord swears revenge. That night you sit outside {npc}'s office door until dawn, and the lamp inside burns red and steady all night, and nobody comes.

choices.text: Advise {npc} to find proof the court will accept

effects.log: "A lamp is not evidence," you say. {npc} smiles tiredly and agrees. It takes a month of digging through the land registers with you holding the lamp. In the end you find the forger, a clerk, and the clerk confesses. The deed is struck down by law. On the last night, the lamp's flame bows, slightly, when {npc} signs the ruling.

events.text: The landlord whose forged deed was struck down has hired killers. You hear of it a day before they come. {npc}, the honest magistrate, refuses to leave the office. "The lamp stays lit," {npc} says, "and so do I."

choices.text: Hold the yamen gate

ok.log: They come at midnight, six of them, over the wall. You hold the inner gate. At the worst of it, the lamp in {npc}'s window flares up so bright the whole courtyard is lit like noon, and the killers, blinded, falter, and that is enough. By dawn they are bound in the yard and the landlord's name is in their mouths. {npc} sends the case to the capital by the lamp's light.

fail.log: They come over the wall and you go down under two of them. But the lamp in {npc}'s window flares up red and blinding, and the rest of them run, shouting that the yamen is on fire, which it is not. {npc} binds your wounds by lamplight and sends the case to the capital in the morning. (-14 health)

choices.text: Take {npc} and the lamp out by the back, and keep moving

effects.log: You take {npc} out by the back gate, lamp and all, and travel by night for a week to the provincial capital, with the lamp lit the whole way, never once guttering in wind or rain. The governor reads the case by its light and has the landlord arrested before the month is out. {npc} never sleeps without the lamp again.

events.text: The dog days, the three hottest of summer, counted on the metal days, when, the old people say, metal hides from fire. Everyone in the village is lying in the shade of the great zelkova. You have been sent up to the high ridge for medicinal herbs, and on the far side of it, in the mouth of a cold cave, you see two eyes, very pale and very large, watching the burning valley with deep dislike.

choices.text: Bow to the cave and go on quietly

effects.log: You bow to the cave mouth and go on quietly with your herbs. The eyes follow you, without interest. At the top of the ridge you look back. Over the valley, very high in the white sky, a red shape is turning in slow circles, and the cave's two pale eyes are fixed on it. You have the distinct impression of two very old neighbours not speaking to each other for the summer.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of cold water at the cave mouth

effects.log: You fill your gourd at the spring and leave the water in a bowl at the cave mouth, keeping a long way back. The eyes regard the bowl. Then, very slowly, something white and huge leans out of the dark and drinks, and you see one stripe, black on white, before it withdraws. In autumn, when the heat breaks, you find the bowl on your doorstep, washed.

events.text: Autumn's first cold morning. The heat has broken overnight. And on the far ridge, at the mouth of the cold cave, you see the pale eyes come out into the light at last, and something white and long stretches, and yawns, and walks out along the ridge as if it owned it. Over the valley, going south, a red glow is leaving, unhurried.

choices.text: Call a greeting to the ridge

effects.log: You call good morning to the ridge, which is a ridiculous thing to do. The white shape stops, and looks at you, and, very slightly, dips its great head. Then it goes on along the ridge into the autumn. You stand in the cool air, laughing, until somebody comes to ask what is the matter.

choices.text: Watch the red glow go south

effects.log: You watch the red glow go, until it is a spark on the horizon, and then nothing. The air is suddenly cold. You understand, standing there, that summer and autumn are not enemies: they are taking turns, very politely, and have been since before there were people to watch them do it.

events.text: Among the heavenly immortals there is a quiet old one, {npc}, who keeps, of all things, a clay fire jar on the terrace of {his} hall, and lays one pine needle on it every morning. You ask about it, at last. "I was the youngest of a house, once, below," {npc} says. "Nine generations of fire, and one cold night it was mine to keep, and there was a spark in the ash that blinked."

choices.text: Ask {npc} what became of the spark

effects.log: "It grew up," {npc} says, smiling. "It went south. It is the bird of the south now, they tell me, and it sits at the council of the Four." A pause. "It has never once come to see me. I do not mind. Fire that is given is not meant to come back." {npc} lays the pine needle on the ash. It curls, and glows.

choices.text: Lay a pine needle on the jar yourself

effects.log: You kneel and lay a pine needle on the ash. {npc} watches with an expression you cannot read. The needle curls and glows, and from somewhere deep in the jar there is a sound, tiny, like a chirp. {npc} goes very still. "It has not done that," {npc} says, "in two thousand years."

events.text: The bird of the south has come to the heavenly halls for the council of the Four. You know where {npc}, the old immortal of the fire jar, will be this evening: on {his} terrace, laying a pine needle on the ash, as always.

choices.text: Tell the bird where to find {npc}

effects.log: You find the great bird after the council and tell it, plainly, where an old immortal keeps a clay fire jar. It goes very quiet. That evening, from your own terrace, you see a red light come down on {npc}'s terrace, small, smaller than you knew it could make itself, the size of a sparrow, and settle on the rim of the jar. You do not watch the rest. Some meetings are for two.

choices.text: Leave it alone: fire that is given is not meant to come back

effects.log: You leave it. {npc} said it: fire that is given is not meant to come back. But that evening, when you pass {npc}'s terrace, the old immortal is sitting by the fire jar with tears on {his} face, and on the rim of the jar, very small, is a red sparrow, and neither of them is saying anything at all.

events.text: In your county the old people have a saying that summer has never once come late, not in a thousand years, and that on the solstice, if you are up before dawn, you can see seven red stars in a line along the south, like a wing being opened. You are up before dawn this solstice, for no reason you can explain. Your chest is tight.

choices.text: Go up the hill and watch the south

effects.log: You go up the hill. Seven red stars, in a line, very faint, opening across the south. As the sun comes up they fade, and a warm wind comes up the valley, and every bird in it starts singing at once. You stand there with tears on your face and no idea why. You feel, absurdly, as if you have been keeping a promise.

choices.text: Light the kitchen fire before anyone else is up

effects.log: You go to the kitchen in the dark and light the fire, carefully, and lay one pine needle on it, which nobody in your house has ever done. The fire takes the needle, and leans toward you, and you would swear, for a moment, it bows. At dawn the summer comes, on time, as always.

events.text: A drought threatens in early summer, and the county's shaman holds a rite to the south. In the middle of it the shaman stops, turns, looks straight at you across the crowd, and says in a voice that is not quite the shaman's own: "Why do you ask me? You know where it sits."

choices.text: Bow to the south, without a word

effects.log: You bow to the south, low, in front of the whole county. The shaman sways, and comes back to themselves, and finishes the rite. The rain does not come. But the heat breaks, gently, over three days, and the millet stands. The shaman avoids you for a year and then, one evening, brings you a jar of wine and asks, quietly, what you remember.

choices.text: Say: I do not know what you mean

effects.log: "I do not know what you mean," you say, and mean it, mostly. The shaman looks at you a moment longer, and then laughs, a laugh like dry sticks catching, and goes back to the rite. That night you dream of a long red wing over the whole south, and of seven small fires under it, and wake warm.

events.text: A great rite in the village, for the five directions: the shaman spins east in blue, west in white, north in black, then takes up the red fan for the south. At the south the shaman spins and spins, faster, the fan a blur of red, and then stops dead, facing you, and falls to the ground on both knees.

choices.text: Help the shaman up

effects.log: You help the shaman up. Their hands are shaking. "Forgive me," they say, very low, so no one else can hear. "I called the south, and the south was standing in the crowd." They press the red fan into your hands and will not take it back. All summer the fan is warm. The village has the best harvest anyone can remember.

choices.text: Back away into the crowd

effects.log: You back away, frightened, and the crowd closes in front of you. The shaman gets up slowly and finishes the rite with eyes shut. But all that summer the heat in your village is exactly right, every day, no more and no less, as if someone were being very careful about it, for your sake.

events.text: Every summer since the rite of the five directions, the first hot day comes to your house before anyone else's. Your hearth is always lit. Your hands are always warm. This summer a stranger from the far north, half frozen in a freak late frost, comes to your gate and says that someone told them to come to you to be warm.

choices.text: Bring them in and sit them by your hearth

effects.log: You sit the stranger by your hearth and the frost comes out of them in an hour, steaming. They tell you that an old woman in their village dreamed of a red emperor, and that the red emperor said: go to the one with the warm hands. You do not know what to say to that. You give them soup.

choices.text: Give them a coal from your hearth to carry home

effects.log: You give them a coal in a clay pot, banked with ash, and tell them about pine needles. They go north with it. A year later a letter comes: the frost has never touched their village since. You keep the letter in the red fan's box.

events.text: A farmer's plough has broken into an old stone tomb on the hill, and the magistrate has sent you down with a lamp to see whether it should be sealed. The walls are painted: a blue dragon to the east, a white tiger to the west, a dark serpent-tortoise to the north. On the south wall, beside the door, a red bird stands on red peaks with a lotus bud in its beak, at the instant of taking flight. On the other side of the door, another, facing it. Same bird. You know that, somehow, the way you know your own hand.

choices.text: Seal the tomb again, gently

effects.log: You report it as an ordinary tomb and have it sealed with earth and turf, gently, the door exactly as it was. As the last of the light goes from the chamber, the two red birds on either side of the door seem, for one breath, to turn their heads and look at you. You walk down the hill and do not look back.

choices.text: Copy the bird by lamplight, every line

effects.log: You sit by the doorway all night copying the bird, line by line, with a brush you did not know you could use so well. The tail curled like a whirlwind. The lotus bud. The peaks. At dawn your copy is better than you could ever have made it. You seal the tomb and keep the copy. Your house has never had a ghost in it since.

events.text: Tomb robbers have dug into the painted tomb on the hill. You hear it from a frightened shepherd: three of them went in at night with lamps, and two came running out screaming about fire at the door, and the third has not come out at all.

choices.text: Go in after the third one

ok.log: You go in with a lamp. The third robber is sitting against the north wall, unhurt, white as rice, staring at the south wall, where two red birds stand on red peaks on either side of the door. "They moved," the robber whispers. "Both of them." You lead the robber out by the hand. The two birds let you pass. The tomb is sealed with stone the next day, and nobody digs there again.

fail.log: You go in and the air at the doorway is hot as an oven mouth, and you stagger back out with your eyebrows singed. A moment later the third robber comes crawling out past you, unhurt, weeping, and confesses everything to the magistrate. The tomb is sealed. You keep your distance from the doorway in your dreams. (-6 health)

choices.text: Tell the magistrate to seal it with stone

effects.log: You go to the magistrate. By the time the magistrate's men arrive, the third robber has come out on their own, at dawn, and is sitting in the field, unhurt, unable to speak of what they saw. The tomb is sealed with stone. The stone, people say, is warm to the touch on the coldest winter day.

events.text: Your family has an heirloom nobody can explain: an old clay fire jar, cracked and mended with wire a dozen times, whose fire has never once gone out, the family says, in a thousand years. Nobody in your line has ever been cold. Sometimes, on very quiet nights, the fire in it chirps. Tonight, when you kneel to bank it, it chirps at you, loudly, three times.

choices.text: Chirp back

effects.log: You chirp back, feeling ridiculous. The fire goes perfectly silent, as if astonished. Then it chirps once more, very softly, and settles. The next morning the whole family wakes warmer than they have ever been. The old woman of the house, at breakfast, looks at you for a long time and says: "It has never answered anyone before."

choices.text: Lay a pine needle on it, the way you somehow know to

effects.log: You lay a pine needle across the ash without thinking. The fire takes it, slowly, like a sleeper turning over, and is still. You have never done that before. Nobody in this house has done it for centuries, the old woman says. She asks where you learned it. You do not know. Your fingers knew.

events.text: A fire has burned down half the village and your family's house with it. Everyone got out. In the black ruins of the kitchen, under the fallen beams, the old fire jar is cracked right through and full of rain. Your family is standing in the yard in silence. The old woman of the house is crying for the first time anyone remembers.

choices.text: Dig the jar out and look inside

effects.log: You dig it out with your hands. It is cracked and full of water. You tip the water out. At the very bottom, in the wet grey ash, one red point. It blinks. You cup it in your hands and carry it to the neighbours' borrowed stove, and it catches there at once, and chirps, and the old woman of the house sits down in the mud and laughs and laughs.

choices.text: Make a new jar, and wait

effects.log: You go to the potter and buy the best jar in the market and set it in the ruined kitchen, empty, and wait, all night, sitting beside it. At dawn there is a red point in the bottom of the new jar that was not there before. You did not put it there. It blinks. Your family's fire has moved house, that is all.

events.text: In the capital, every evening for five hundred years, one fire has burned on the southern hill: all is well. Everyone looks at it without seeing it, like the moon. You cannot stop seeing it. Every evening it lights, you feel it, here, under your ribs, like a breath let out. Tonight it is late.

choices.text: Climb the southern hill to see why
