effects.log: You climb the hill in the dark. At the beacon mound the soldiers are standing round a cold chimney, the wood soaked by an afternoon storm, swearing. As you come up, the wood in the chimney catches by itself, all at once, with a sound like a breath. The soldiers jump back. One fire. All is well. You go back down feeling, absurdly, that you have done your duty.

choices.text: Wait in your lane and watch the hill

effects.log: You wait in the lane, watching the dark hill, with your heart thudding. Then it lights, late, but bright, brighter than you have ever seen it, and the breath under your ribs goes out, and you sit down on your doorstep. A neighbour asks if you are ill. You say you were only waiting for the beacon. The neighbour looks at you very strangely.

events.text: Tonight, for the first time in your life, the southern hill above the capital shows two fires. Then three. The city stirs. And you, without knowing how, know where the trouble is: on the southern coast, at a river mouth, three days' ride away. You can almost see the sails.

choices.text: Go to the Ministry of War and tell them where

ok.log: You get in to see a duty officer, and tell them the river mouth, and the number of sails. They laugh at you. Then the runners come in from the beacon road and say the same river mouth, and the same number. The officer looks at you very differently. The raid is met at the river mouth. You are asked, politely, never to explain yourself, and you do not.

fail.log: You try, and are thrown out of the ministry for a madman. The raid is met at the river mouth anyway, two days later, by the coast troops. You were right. Nobody ever knows it but you. The beacon on the southern hill shows one fire again on the fifth night, and you sleep for the first time in a week.

choices.text: Climb the southern hill and stand by the fire

effects.log: You climb the hill and stand by the three fires all night with the soldiers. You do not know why you came. Toward dawn the third fire dies down, by itself, to two, and then, as the sun comes up, to one. The soldiers look at you. You look back. One of them, an old one, bows to you, and does not say why.

events.text: Swallows love your house. Every spring, on the third day of the third month, they come back to your eaves before anyone else's, more of them than any house in the county, and the old people say a house the swallows love is a kind house. This spring the first swallow back flies straight in through your open door and drops something in your lap.

choices.text: Plant it

effects.log: It is a gourd seed. You plant it by the wall. The gourds that grow are full of rice, and the swallows nest under your eaves all summer, chattering at you as if you were one of them. You understand, though you could not say how, that this is a thank-you, and that it comes from very far south.

choices.text: Give it to the poorest house you know

effects.log: You give it to the poorest house you know, and tell them to plant it. The gourds are full of rice. The next spring, two swallows come to that house too, the first swallows it has ever had, and the poor family stands under the eaves weeping. Your own swallows come back, as always, and seem pleased with you.

events.text: A cruel landlord in the next village has heard about the gourd seeds and has had every swallow's nest in his house knocked down, and is waiting, he says, for the swallows to bring him what he is owed. This spring, every swallow in the county is circling your roof, hundreds of them, as if waiting for you to decide something.

choices.text: Tell the swallows: leave him be; he will learn

effects.log: You stand in your yard and say it out loud to the swallows, feeling foolish. They wheel away. The landlord gets no seeds at all, ever. In the end, years later, you hear he put up a nest-shelf under his eaves, and waited, and waited, and one spring a single young swallow nested on it. He wept, they say. He gave the village a well.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: You say nothing. The swallows decide for themselves. That autumn the landlord plants a gourd seed he found on his step, and the gourds are full of hornets, as in the old story. You are not sorry. You are not glad either. You go and help the village with the hornets.

events.text: In a merchant's shop in the provincial town there is a vase in a case of its own: the Kingfisher Vase, jade-green, a colour no kiln has made in three hundred years, since the secret was lost. Buyers come from the capital to look at it. When you walk past the case, the vase rings, faintly, like a struck bell. The merchant turns pale.

choices.text: Ask to hold it

effects.log: The merchant, shaking, lets you. It is warm in your hands, warm as an egg under a hen. You know, holding it, exactly how it was fired: forty hours of pine, the reducing smoke, the hottest place in the firebox and what sat there. You give it back. The merchant asks you, in a whisper, if you are a potter. You say no. You are not sure that is true.

choices.text: Walk on quickly

effects.log: You walk on quickly. Behind you the vase stops ringing. That night you dream of a white-hot firebox and of lying down in it, warm and tired and happy, while a potter sings outside. You wake with ash on your pillow and no idea where it came from.

events.text: A poor potter's family on the southwest coast has heard that a person in your town made the Kingfisher Vase ring. They have come to you, shy, with three failed pots, all muddy grey-green, to ask if you know anything about the old colour. They have tried for three generations.

choices.text: Go with them and sit by their kiln through a firing

effects.log: You go. You sit by their firebox through forty hours of firing, telling them things you did not know you knew: where the heat should sit, when to close the ports, how the smoke should smell. When the kiln is opened, one pot of thirty is green, not the old colour, but nearer than anyone has come in three hundred years. The family cries. So, a little, do you.

choices.text: Tell them honestly: some secrets are meant to be lost

effects.log: "Some things are meant to be lost," you say, and you do not know why you are so sure. The family is disappointed, and goes home. A year later they send you a bowl, their own colour, a muddy honest green. It is beautiful in its own way. You use it every day. You think whoever made the old colour would be pleased.

events.text: On the southern island, they say, there is a star you can see from nowhere else in the land: the Old Man Star, low on the sea in winter, red-white, and whoever sees it lives long. You have come to the island on an errand, and on your last night an old fisherman takes you to the shore to look. When it rises, it is so familiar that you cannot breathe.

choices.text: Look at it until it sets

effects.log: You watch it until it sets, and all that time it seems to watch you back, warm, the way a lamp in a window watches a road. The old fisherman says nothing. When it is gone he says: "My grandmother said it was a bird once. A red one, from the north, that flew too far." You go home with a cough you have had for years gone. (+10 health)

choices.text: Ask the old fisherman how old he is

effects.log: "Ninety-eight," he says. "I have seen it every winter of my life." He looks at the star, and then at you. "It never flickers like that for me," he says. "It is flickering at you." It is. You watch it until dawn. You live, in the end, to be very old.

events.text: Your old friend from the southern island, the fisherman who showed you the Old Man Star, is dying, well past a hundred, and has sent for you. When you arrive it is a clear winter night, and the star is up over the sea, very bright.

choices.text: Carry him down to the shore to see it

effects.log: You carry him down to the black rocks wrapped in every quilt in the house. He watches the star a long time. "Every winter," he says. "Thank you for coming." You are not sure he is speaking to you. He dies at dawn, easily, with the star just setting into the sea. You stay on the island until spring.

choices.text: Sit with him, and tell him what the star is

effects.log: You tell him, as plainly as you can, what you dreamed the star is: a red bird that flew south so far it became a fire for long lives. He listens, delighted, like a child. "I knew it," he says. "I always said it was looking at me." He dies that night. On the shore, the star is very bright.

events.text: In the capital, the south gate's name-board hangs on end, not across, and there is a square pond before it, and stone fire-eaters at the palace door, all because of the sharp peak to the south, the fire mountain, which the geomancers say has something on it. Every child in the city knows it. Every time you pass the pond, you want, very badly, to laugh, and also to cry, and you do not know why.

choices.text: Climb the fire mountain

effects.log: You climb it on a summer day. At the top, in a hollow of bare rock, the stone is warm, much warmer than the sun can make it, in the exact shape of a great bird lying down. You lie down in it. You can see the whole capital from there: the pond, the gate, the palace. Everything is watching you, and you are watching everything. You fall asleep. You wake at dusk, perfectly happy.

choices.text: Throw a coin in the pond, as people do, for luck

effects.log: You throw a coin in the pond. The water, which is always cool, is warm where the coin goes in, as if you had thrown in a coal. The carp come to look at you. On the mountain, at that moment, people say afterwards, there was a red flash at the summit, like somebody waving.

events.text: A drought summer, and the pond before the south gate has dried to a puddle. The geomancers are frantic: the fire mountain will burn the city now, they say, with no water to face it. There has already been one fire, in a market lane. The city is frightened.

choices.text: Carry water to the pond, bucket after bucket, all day

effects.log: You carry water from the river to the pond all day, alone, and then not alone: a child joins you, then a water-seller, then half the lane. By evening the pond is full again. At dusk the fire mountain glows, faintly, and then dims, gently, like a lamp being turned down out of courtesy. There are no more fires that summer.

choices.text: Tell people the mountain is not their enemy

ok.log: You stand by the dry pond and tell the frightened crowd what you somehow know: the mountain guards the city as much as it threatens it; the fire in the market lane was a dyer's careless brazier. They listen, more than you expected. That night it rains, for the first time in two months. The geomancers claim the credit.

fail.log: You try and are shouted down as a fool. But that night, very late, it rains, and the pond fills, and in the morning the summit of the fire mountain is wreathed in a mist that smells, faintly, of steam and of laughter.

events.text: There is a county in the south where nothing grows on the hills: old black stumps, a thousand years old, and thin grass. The swallows never come back to it in spring. People say a fire once ran over one mountain and the next and did not stop. You were sent there on an errand, and you cannot leave. Every black stump makes you ashamed.

choices.text: Plant a pine on the bare slope

effects.log: You buy a pine seedling at the market and carry it up the black hill and plant it, and water it from the stream. It is a silly thing to do. You do it anyway. The next spring you come back and it is alive. You plant ten more. You keep coming back for the rest of your life, and by the end the hill above that village is green, and you are not ashamed any more.

choices.text: Ask the old people of the county what happened

effects.log: The old people tell you: a red bird gave the south fire, and gave too much, and forgot, and kept its temper too long, and one day it all ran wild. "It was not wicked," one old woman says. "It was careless. That is worse, and it is also better." You do not ask her what she means. You think you know.

events.text: You have been coming back to the burned county for years, planting trees. This spring, on the third day of the third month, an old man runs up the hill to fetch you, crying. Under the eaves of the headman's house, for the first time in a thousand years, there is a swallow.

choices.text: Go and look

effects.log: You go and look. One swallow, one mud nest, half built. The whole village stands in the headman's yard in silence, watching it work. You stand with them. When you go home that evening, the black hills are green on one side, your side, and you feel something lift off you that you have carried since before you were born.

choices.text: Keep planting: one swallow is not a spring

effects.log: "One swallow is not a spring," you say, which is an old saying, and go on planting. But your hands shake. That summer there are three nests. The next, eleven. By the time you are old the county is full of swallows and green hills, and nobody remembers it was ever black, except you, and you are glad to be the only one.

events.text: In your county summer always comes late, a month late, the old people say, ever since some old thing happened that nobody can name. And in a ruined house at the edge of the village, roofless, abandoned for centuries, there is an old cold fire jar that nobody will move. You find yourself standing over it in the snow, with pine needles in your hand.

choices.text: Lay a needle on the cold ash

effects.log: You lay one pine needle on the cold grey ash. Nothing. You stay kneeling a long time anyway, in the snow. Then, very faintly, so faintly you might have imagined it, the needle curls at one end, and a thread of smoke goes up from it, one breath long, and stops. That year summer comes a week earlier than it has in living memory.

choices.text: Carry the jar home to your own kitchen

effects.log: You carry the cold jar home through the snow and set it by your own stove, where it is warm. Your family thinks you have gone mad. For a month, nothing. Then, one morning, the ash in it is warm to the touch, and there is a single grey feather on top of it, and your kitchen smells of summer.

events.text: You have kept the cold jar by your stove for years now, laying a needle on it every night. This winter, on the coldest night of the year, you wake with a start. In the dark kitchen, in the grey ash of the old jar, one red point. It blinks.

choices.text: Breathe on it, very gently

effects.log: You breathe on it, the softest breath of your life. It swells, and shakes itself, and somewhere in the ash something goes chirp, small and hoarse and astonished. By dawn there is a fire in the old jar for the first time in centuries. That summer, in your county, summer comes on time. The old people do not know what to make of it. You do.

choices.text: Wake the whole house to see

effects.log: You wake everyone, and they come stumbling into the kitchen in their quilts, grumbling, and stop. A red point in the grey ash, blinking. The youngest of the house, without being told, lays a pine needle on it, and it catches, and chirps. Everyone is crying, and nobody knows why, and summer comes on time.

events.text: Over the door of the old house where you lodge there is a talisman, very old, written in a red so bright it seems to glow at night. No ghost has come near that house in five hundred years, the family says: the ink is the famous red, ground from a bird. When you look at it, your whole body hurts, deep in the bones, as if you had been ground too.

choices.text: Take it down, carefully, and burn it in the hearth

effects.log: You ask the family's leave, and they give it, frightened. You take the talisman down and lay it in the hearth. It burns red, and long, far longer than paper, and the flame is shaped, for one moment, like a wing opening. Then it is ash. Your bones stop hurting. The house has no ghost that year anyway. Perhaps it never needed one.

choices.text: Leave it: it is still protecting the house

effects.log: You leave it. It is still doing what it was made to do, whatever it cost. You sleep under it every night of your stay, and your bones ache, and you dream of a mortar, and you wake each morning to children laughing safely in a house no ghost has touched. You do not know what to feel. Both, perhaps.

events.text: An alchemist's shop in the capital has the last of the old red ink: one stoppered jar, kept in a locked box, sold a drop at a time to great houses for a fortune. You have come, without meaning to, and are standing at the counter. The jar, in its box, is warm. You can feel it from here.

choices.text: Buy the whole jar, whatever it costs, and pour it in the sea

effects.log: It costs thirty taels, everything you have. You carry it to the southern sea and pour it into the waves at noon on the solstice. The red spreads on the water like a wing, and for one breath the whole sea is vermilion, and warm, and then it is just the sea. You walk home poor and lighter than you have ever been.

choices.text: Ask the alchemist where it came from

effects.log: The alchemist tells you, as one might tell a fine story: a net on a southern cliff, a mortar, nine days, mercury. The alchemist's great-grandparent's work. "A whole bird," the alchemist says proudly. You walk out without a word. That night you cannot stop shaking. In the morning you go and warn every dealer in the medicine market that the red birds of the south are not for sale, and some of them, oddly, listen.

choices.text: Walk out

effects.log: You walk out, fast, and do not go down that street again. But for the rest of your life, whenever you see a talisman in that red over a door, you bow to it, a little, as you would at a grave.

events.text: You have always had a dangerous laugh. When you really laugh, hard, something catches: a lamp flares, a paper window singes, once a whole straw mat smouldered. Your family hides the lamps when guests are funny. Tonight, at a village feast, a neighbour is telling the story of the magistrate and the goat, and it is very, very funny.

choices.text: Swallow the laugh

effects.log: You swallow it. It goes down hot as soup and sits in your chest, smouldering. You go red, and your eyes water, and the neighbour, delighted, tells the next bit. You swallow that too. By the end of the evening you have a fever. The old woman of the house puts you to bed and says, darkly, that swallowed laughter has to come out somewhere. (-3 health)

choices.text: Run outside and laugh at the sky

effects.log: You run out into the yard and laugh at the sky, hard, until you cry. A cloud overhead turns faintly pink at the edges. Nothing catches. You come back in to find everyone looking at you, and laugh again, and this time you have learned something: it is only dangerous indoors.

choices.text: Sing instead

effects.log: Without knowing why, you start to sing instead: the goat, the magistrate, the whole story, as a song. The laugh goes into the song and out through it, and the lamps flicker but do not flare. The whole feast joins the chorus. The old woman of the house looks at you as if she had just seen something very old in your face.

events.text: A pompous official from the capital is inspecting your county, and has said, in front of everyone, one word too many about your village. Everyone is looking at you, because everyone knows about your laugh. You can feel it coming up from somewhere very deep, older than you.

choices.text: Sing it out: a song about the official, there and then

effects.log: You sing. A song about the official, his hat, his horse, his one word too many, made up on the spot. The village roars. The official goes purple and then, against his will, laughs too. Nothing catches. The song is sung in your county for generations, and you have never felt so light.

choices.text: Swallow it, for the village's sake

effects.log: You swallow it, for the village. It burns all the way down. The official finishes his inspection and leaves, and that night the old stone of your hearth cracks across, with a sound like a laugh, and you sit by it, feeling better. Not every fire has to burn an archive. Some can just crack a stone. (-5 health)

events.text: In your valley there is an old rite nobody else keeps: on the first cool day of autumn, the farmers leave a bowl of new rice on a stone facing the western mountains, to thank whoever brought autumn back, once, long ago, when summer would not end. You have never been able to watch it without feeling sick with shame. This year you are asked to carry the bowl.

choices.text: Carry it, and say thank you to the west

effects.log: You carry the bowl to the stone and set it down facing west and say thank you, out loud. Your voice cracks. The farmers look at you, puzzled. A cool wind comes down from the western mountains, very clean, smelling of pine and snow, and touches your face like a hand, and the shame goes. In its place: autumn. You had never noticed how beautiful it is.

choices.text: Ask why the summer would not end

effects.log: "Something held it," the oldest farmer says. "Something that loved it too much. Summer is a guest. You have to let a guest go home." You carry the bowl in silence. On the way back, for the first time in your life, you are glad the leaves are turning.

events.text: A hot autumn: the heat will not break, the wells are low, the rice is drying in the fields. The farmers are frightened. You stand in the cracked paddy at noon and feel, very clearly, that you could keep it this way if you wanted to: that something in you is holding on to the summer, and could hold on longer.

choices.text: Let it go

effects.log: You let go. You do not know how. You just do, the way you open a fist. That evening a cool wind comes down from the west, and in the night it rains, and in the morning the paddies are full and the leaves are turning. You sleep for two days. When you wake, you are not afraid of autumn any more.

choices.text: Go west to the mountains and ask

effects.log: You walk west to the mountains, three days, and at the top of the first pass, in a cold wind, you stand and say out loud: "I am sorry. Take it." Nothing answers. But on the walk back the air is cool, and the paddies, when you get home, are full of water, and the farmers say the heat broke the day you left.

events.text: On the coldest night of the year you cannot sleep, and go to the kitchen, and kneel by the fire jar. In the grey ash there is one red point. It is not an ember. It blinks. And you know, with absolute certainty, that it remembers you, and that it knows that you remember it.

choices.text: Say: I know

effects.log: "I know," you whisper. The red point blinks, twice. Then it settles into the ash, and the fire jar is warm, and the kitchen is warm, and you go back to bed and sleep like a child. In the morning there is nothing in the jar but a good bed of coals. You are not sad. You know where it is.

choices.text: Feed it a pine needle

effects.log: You lay a pine needle across it. It takes the needle, quickly, greedily, like someone who has been very hungry for a very long time, and then chirps, very small. You sit by the jar till dawn. You think: this time, it will be different. You do not know what you mean by that. It does.

events.text: Years after the night of the spark, on a summer evening, a small red bird lands on your windowsill. It is much too young to be anything at all: a red sparrow, really, nothing more. It looks at you exactly the way the spark did.

choices.text: Tell it, quietly, to be careful with its temper this time

effects.log: "Be careful with your temper," you say, quietly, "this time." The little bird ruffles every feather, offended, and then, after a moment, seems to think about it. It sits on your windowsill until dark. When it flies, it flies south, low and careful, and does not set a single thing alight on the way.

choices.text: Hold out a crumb of rice cake

effects.log: You hold out a crumb of rice cake. It hops onto your finger, eats it, and is so hot your finger blisters, and you do not move. It looks up at you. Then it is gone. You keep the blister like a secret. You hope, very much, that this time it gets everything right.
